Statement : The blocking of BitChat's code on GitHub is unconstitutional and authoritarian. 

New Delhi, 24 July 2026

The Internet Freedom Foundation (IFF) condemns the order issued by the Indian Cyber Crime Coordination Centre (I4C), Ministry of Home Affairs, directing GitHub to remove the code repositories of BitChat. 

The order, Notice No. 11072601011432, was issued at 11:16 pm on 23 July 2026 under Section 79(3)(b) of the Information Technology Act, 2000 read with Rule 3(1)(d) of the IT Rules, 2021. The order directs GitHub to disable access to three repositories, including the Android application and its release files, within three hours. It threatens the platform with loss of safe harbour and criminal prosecution. No copy was published by the Government of India. The public learnt of it from a post by @jack, whose team develops BitChat. Censorship in India now comes to light through disclosure by the censored.

Since 17 July 2026, the Ministry of Home Affairs has suspended mobile internet around Jantar Mantar as per public reports about five times, most recently within a 1.5 kilometre radius from 4 pm until midnight on 23 July. That radius takes in Janpath and parts of Connaught Place. Reports describe signal jammers at the protest site and people walking two kilometres before their phones work. Inside that zone a student separated from her group during a detention drive cannot send a message to say where she is. Thousands of students and young people have camped at Jantar Mantar since June, seeking accountability for examination irregularities. Permission for their march to Parliament was refused. Metro stations were shut and also internet connectivity has been blocked.

BitChat is an open source application built for exactly this situation. It passes messages from phone to phone over Bluetooth, without mobile networks or a central server. It is striking that the order does not identify a single unlawful message. It objects to what BitChat is. In its own words, the application is dangerous because it enables communication "even during network restrictions" and can "circumvent lawful restrictions" during "internet shutdowns". Hence, the government's objection is that citizens can speak to one another while it has switched the internet off. 

The order is illegal on at least four grounds. 

1. Section 79(3)(b) is not a blocking power. In Shreya Singhal v. Union of India (2015) 5 SCC 1, the Supreme Court read down the provision. Intermediaries may be required to act only on a court order, or a government notification confined to the grounds under Article 19(2) of the Constitution. Blocking is governed exclusively by Section 69A and the Blocking Rules, 2009, which require a hearing and reasons recorded in writing, subject to review. Directions issued under Section 79(3)(b), Rule 3(1)(d) and the Sahyog Portal evade these safeguards, and constitutional challenges to this parallel regime are pending before High Courts. 

2. The reasons in the order are circular. The order asserts that the repositories contain "information which is prohibited under any law" without naming any such information, and rests on what the application is "capable of" enabling. Anticipated misuse of a communications tool is not a lawful basis to prohibit the tool. By this logic a telephone exchange could be sealed. 

3. The order cites Section 43 of the IT Act, a civil compensation provision, alongside conspiracy and abetment offences under the Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita, 2023, against a platform that hosts code. 

4. A three hour deadline issued close to midnight forecloses legal assessment and recourse, and fails the proportionality standard in Anuradha Bhasin v. Union of India (2020) 3 SCC 637.

The order also fails on its own terms as deleting a repository does not delete the application from any phone that carries it, and the mesh keeps functioning without servers. What the takedown actually prevents is scrutiny of the underlying code.

IFF demands that the Government of India:

1. Withdraw Notice No. 11072601011432 dated 23 July 2026 issued to GitHub.
2. Publish every takedown direction issued under Section 79(3)(b), Rule 3(1)(d) and the Sahyog Portal, with the reasons recorded for each.
3. Restore full connectivity around Jantar Mantar, publish all suspension orders, and disclose the legal authority for the deployment of jammers.

We stand with the developers and the young protesters whose speech this order seeks to silence.

text:
Statement on the Indian government's order to GitHub to block BitChat:

The Indian Cyber Crime Coordination Centre (@Cyberdost ) under the Ministry of Home Affairs (@PIBHomeAffairs) has ordered GitHub (@github) to remove three URLs linking to BitChat, an app that works offline without an internet connection and enables users to communicate over Bluetooth. This order was issued under Section 79(3)(b) of the Information Technology Act, 2000, read with Rule 3(1)(d) of the Information Technology (Intermediary Guidelines and Digital Media Ethics Code) Rules, 2021.

During the internet shutdowns imposed on multiple occasions over the past week in parts of Central Delhi, many protesters faced difficulties communicating or seeking emergency services. Open-source applications like BitChat allow people to communicate with other people using the same application nearby, without an internet connection.

The order states that the application would impede the state's ability to conduct lawful interception and surveillance and enable users to circumvent lawful restrictions such as internet shutdowns. The notice was issued at 11:16 PM on 23rd July and has given GitHub three hours to remove the links.

However, the order fails to satisfy the tests of legality, necessity, and proportionality and constitutes as an abject misuse of Section 79(3)(b) of the IT Act, read with Rule 3(1)(d) of the IT Rules 2021.

At the outset, Section 79(3)(b) does not confer the power to block or remove content, which instead stems from Section 69A of the IT Act. The issuance of orders with generic grounds is further inconsistent with the safeguards laid down by the Supreme Court in Shreya Singhal v. Union of India. The Supreme Court upheld Section 69A of the IT Act, 2000 strictly because it required that blocking orders must be reasoned, necessary, and proportionate, and that such reasons must be recorded in writing to enable judicial review.

The opacity surrounding these removals goes against the strict requirements of accountability and record-keeping embedded in the Information Technology (Procedure and Safeguards for Blocking for Access of Information by Public) Rules, 2009.

The only reason this particular order in the current instance became public is not due to dissemination by the issuing authority, but rather because @Jack posted about the same on X. What we see emerging through these removals is a system of informal, decentralised censorship, where the government can direct content removals without transparency or oversight.

The lack of information renders a meaningful legal challenge impossible and leaves affected parties without legal redressal, including the basic elements of review that Section 69A provides when read with the Blocking Rules 2009. Orders passed under Section 79(3)(b) therefore function as circumventions of the procedural safeguards enumerated under Section 69A of the IT Act.

@jack @BitchatMe_ @callebtc @FOSSUnited @GitHubPolicy @GithubProjects

#FOSS #internetshutdown

text:
IFF statement against the Alarming Escalation of Social Media Censorship and Proposed Expansion of Takedown Powers

New Delhi, March 19, 2026

The Internet Freedom Foundation (IFF) is concerned by continuing reports of posts and accounts being withheld in India on Facebook, X and Instagram, including satire and criticism of the government. Recent reporting shows users receiving generic “withheld in India” notices or emails under Section 69A from social media platforms, with little or no explanation, while independent reporting has documented takedowns affecting speech that appears political, satirical, or critical rather than clearly unlawful.

As reported by Business Standard and The Indian Express on March 18, the Union Government is currently exploring a proposal to decentralize content blocking powers under Section 69A of the IT Act. The new proposal would grant direct takedown powers to multiple ministries, including Defence, Home Affairs, External Affairs, and Information & Broadcasting. At present, MeitY signs off on Section 69A orders, while a separate notice and takedown channel already operates through Section 79(3)(b) and the Home Ministry led Sahyog portal that at least has 35 nodal officers across State Police Departments in India.

At the same time, the February 2026 amendments to the IT Rules have sharply compressed compliance timelines. MeitY’s own published FAQ says intermediaries must act within 3 hours when they receive actual knowledge through a court order or a government intimation, within 36 hours for certain expedited grievances, and within 2 hours for specified complaints involving nudity, sexual content, morphed content, and impersonation. The government has also reiterated that intermediaries which fail to observe due diligence risk losing Section 79 immunity. A system built on speed, legal threat, and secrecy predictably incentivises over compliance.

We remind the Union Government that the Supreme Court upheld Section 69A in the Shreya Singhal case on the basis of procedural safeguards and written reasons that could be challenged. Secret and inaccessible censorship defeats those safeguards in practice. 

IFF calls on the Union government to halt any move to decentralise Section 69A blocking powers further, publish blocking orders with only as per the letter and spirit of the Shreya Singhal judgement, and ensure timely notice to affected users with clear grounds and avenues for remedy. Platforms must also do more than send boilerplate messages. They should provide meaningful notice, preserve records for challenge, and publish granular transparency reporting given online censorship also impacts the public right to receive information.

If your account or post has been withheld or blocked in India, please write to legal@internetfreedom.in with screenshots, URLs, and any email or platform notice you have received. IFF will try to assist impacted users and document patterns of opaque censorship.

text:
The Delhi Police's takedown drive against posts critical of the Prime Minister is unconstitutional. 

New Delhi, 27 July 2026

Media reports today state that the Delhi Police has directed social media platforms to remove posts, videos, memes and reels containing remarks it describes as "abusive", "offensive" and "objectionable" towards the Prime Minister, uploaded during the student protests at Jantar Mantar and after the 'Sansad Chalo' march of 20 July 2026. At least three platforms have reportedly received notices. Several posts have already been taken down. A dedicated police team is monitoring social media to identify further content, and reports indicate that criminal proceedings are contemplated against those who posted it. No order has been published. While reports indicate the notices invoke the Information Technology Act, the specific provision relied upon and the text of the notices remain undisclosed. 

The Internet Freedom Foundation condemns this takedown drive and calls for the notices to be disclosed and withdrawn.

On the reports available, the content being removed is political expression. The movement at Jantar Mantar has been conducted as much through reels, memes, posters and digital artwork as through assembly on the ground. This is how a digital native generation raised online speaks about accountability. As per Article 19(2) restrictions on speech only on eight specified grounds. Offensiveness is not one of them. In Shreya Singhal v. Union of India (2015) 5 SCC 1, the Supreme Court struck down Section 66A of the IT Act precisely because expressions such as "grossly offensive" and causing "annoyance" were vague, subjective, and swept protected speech within their net. Eleven years later, the Delhi Police is applying the same standard through informal notices and legal powers which are not being publicly disclosed. 

As per existing practices there are two routes for removing online content. The first is Section 69A of the IT Act read with the Blocking Rules, 2009, which requires a reasoned order, committee review, and notice to the originator, as the Delhi High Court affirmed in Tanul Thakur v. Union of India (2022). The second is Section 79(3)(b), which Shreya Singhal read down to require a court order or a government notification strictly confined to Article 19(2) grounds. If these notices were routed through the Sahyog Portal, they rest on a regime whose constitutionality remains under challenge before multiple High Courts. However, even if it is used police notices citing offensiveness satisfy neither. 

Reports that platforms were told the content violates "their policies" make the defect worse, the police have no mandate to enforce the community guidelines of private companies. Unpublished directions are also contrary to Anuradha Bhasin v. Union of India (2020) 3 SCC 637, which requires that orders restricting fundamental rights be published so that they can be challenged. If the underlying theory is defamation of the Prime Minister, the police have no role at all. Defamation under Section 356 of the BNS is a non-cognizable offence, prosecuted only on a complaint by the person aggrieved under Section 222 of the BNSS. 

Our demands

1. The Delhi Police must publish every notice issued, the legal provision invoked, and the list of URLs affected.

2. Notices directed at satire, criticism, and political commentary must be withdrawn. Any removal must follow the procedures under Section 69A or a judicial order.

3. No criminal proceedings should be initiated against persons for speech that does not meet the constitutional threshold of incitement.

4. Platforms must decline requests unsupported by valid legal orders, notify affected users, and disclose the number of government demands in their transparency reports.

Students who question an examination system are exercising their fundamental rights and deleting their posts will not delete their questions.

Reports referred to:

1. Times of India, "Delhi Police orders removal of offensive posts against PM Narendra Modi linked to NEET paper leak protests", 27 July 2026
2. News18, "Delhi Police Issues Notices To Social Media Platforms Over Offensive Posts Against PM Modi During Jantar Mantar Protest", 27 July 2026

Statement : Shutting down Telegram is a band aid solution and is a disproportionate answer to exam fraud

The Internet Freedom Foundation objects to the directions announced today in the National Testing Agency's press release on action against the Telegram platform. On the NTA's recommendation, the Ministry of Electronics and Information Technology has, under Section 69A of the Information Technology Act, 2000, restricted access to the whole of Telegram in India until 22 June 2026, and has separately ordered the platform to switch off message-editing for every Indian user until 30 June 2026. This is a blunt, nationwide measure aimed at the conduct of rampant fraud rackets, and on the Government's own admission is constitutionally incompatible.

At the outset it is important to note that Section 69A and the Blocking Rules of 2009 framed under it allow the Government to block access to specific “information” on a computer resource. They do not extend to switching off an entire intermediary, still less to ordering a company to redesign its product by removing a feature for a whole country. In Shreya Singhal v Union of India, the Supreme Court upheld Section 69A because it is narrow and hedged with procedural safeguards. Reading it to authorise shutting down a platform that lakhs use is an overbroad restriction by the NTAs own admission. For the message-editing direction the release identifies no source of power at all. If one exists, the order must say so.

The release argues against itself

A restriction on access has to be the least intrusive measure that achieves its aim as per the constitutional test of proportionality laid down in Justice K.S. Puttaswamy v. Union of India (2017) and applied in Anuradha Bhasin v. Union of India (2020). The NTA's own narration shows the block fails its nodal agency, the release says, “has secured the prompt take-down of a substantial number of Telegram channels, groups and bots”, and this targeted work “is the reason the harm caused by these rackets has been contained to the extent it has”. If channel level takedown contained the harm, the case for a blanket block collapses and hence the Government has reached for a heavier tool while conceding that a lighter one was working. The collateral cost sits on the record too as noted in the press release. The block, the NTA accepts, “affects lakhs of citizens who use the Telegram platform for legitimate personal, educational, professional and informational purposes”. The release also says there is "no such paper available outside the secured examination chain" and that “the security of the examination is unaffected by the action taken”. If the exam is secure and no leak exists, what is being suppressed is rumour, and rumour cannot justify closing a platform when specific blocking and criminal prosecution remain available.

Students use of Telegram

The block of telegram is reactive and ineffective and will punish ordinary users instead of addressing the systemic source of exam leaks. This blocking comes in the final days of NEET preparation, when thousands of students depend on Telegram for study groups, doubt-clearing, and shared resources. Also, it is important to consider that the source of exam papers leak will occur from inside the system, among insiders and across the printing and logistics chain, with the platform being the most downstream channel for distribution. Hence, switching off Telegram, is merely a deflection from the repeated failures that will continue while media attention is directed towards this Telegram ban.

Lack of transparency

At present only a press release from the NTA has been provided, which recommended the block but the reasoned order of MeitY, the authority that issued it, has not been released. The Anuradha Bhasin decision requires that orders restricting access be published so they can be tested in court. Here the order, and the reasoning of the committee behind it, stay out of view, and we do not know whether Telegram was heard at all. An announcement of a block is no substitute for an order the affected party can challenge.
Blunt to enforce and very easy to evade
Usually, app-level blocks run through IS-level DNS and IP filtering. They are over inclusive, sweeping in lawful use, yet simple to evade as a determined exam leak racket moves to a VPN or a mirror within minutes while ordinary users lose the service for a week.

We ask the Government to:

1) Publish the MeitY Section 69A order and the NTA recommendation behind it, with reasons;
2) State the legal basis for the message editing direction, or withdraw it;
3) Confirm whether Telegram was given a hearing under the Blocking Rules, and place the committee's record before any court that hears a challenge; and
4) Lift the platform-wide restriction and rely on the targeted takedowns the NTA itself credits with containing the harm.

We emphasise that the NEET (UG) 2026 re-examination is worth protecting and it concerns the future of lakhs of aspirants. It requires securing the entire process of examination rather than reaching for purported band aid solutions that instead cause more harm. The State cannot switch off a service used by lakhs to answer the wrongdoing of a few, and cannot do it through an order no one affected is allowed to read. Statement on MeitY's notice to WhatsApp over the "usernames" feature

The Ministry of Electronics and Information Technology (MeitY) has sent WhatsApp a notice about the usernames feature it announced on 29 June 2026. The notice asks the company to explain, within three days, why regulatory action should not be taken against it "for launching a feature that may increase cybercrimes", and it directs the company "not to roll out this feature until the consultation on this point is achieved to the satisfaction of the Government". The Internet Freedom Foundation is concerned that the notice has no clear basis in law. It is an attempt by the executive to decide what a company may build and ship, which no statute permits.

The notice treats the launch of a lawful feature as a wrong the company must justify. That reverses the ordinary position especially given the absence of any clear legal power that exists. MeitY does not name any provision that lets it approve a product feature before release or order one withdrawn, because there is none, and the provisions it does cite do not supply that power.

Section 79 of the IT Act, 2000 is a safe harbour that protects an intermediary from liability for what its users post, so long as it observes due diligence. It decides when a platform can be held liable. It is not a power for MeitY to decide what features the platform may offer. Sections 66C and 66D punish identity theft and cheating by personation. They are criminal offences, tried by courts, aimed at the person who steals an identity, not at the maker of a tool that a third party misuses. Also, on MeitY's logic, a telecom operator could be told not to sell SIM cards because SIM cards are used in almost every online fraud. 

Rule 3(1)(b), Rule 3(2) and Rule 4 of the IT Rules, 2021 are due diligence and grievance obligations and cannot be converted into a licensing scheme. Section 69A, the one provision that lets MeitY control what appears online, permits the blocking of specific information through a set procedure. It says nothing about which features a company may build. Further the IT Rules, 2021 are subordinate legislation made under Sections 79 and 87 of the IT Act, and subordinate rules cannot travel beyond the parent statute (Ajoy Kumar Banerjee v. Union of India). If a rule cannot exceed the Act, a letter certainly cannot. The power to require prior permission for a feature is not in the Act, not in the Rules, and cannot be created by a notice. 

MeitY has tried this before. In March 2024 it told the same large intermediaries, among them AI Companies, to obtain its explicit permission before deploying under-tested AI models. That was criticised as an overreach that sought to build a licensing mechanism with no empowering provision in the IT Act, and within a fortnight MeitY withdrew it and dropped the permission requirement. This notice repeats the move for a single feature and goes further, because it names one company, sets a three-day clock, and bars the launch until MeitY is satisfied. 

This matters beyond WhatsApp. A power asserted against one company by letter can be turned on any company and any feature. On this reasoning MeitY could tell a browser not to switch on a privacy setting by default, or a payments app not to add a login method, each time until it was content. The notice also invokes traceability, through Rule 4(2) of the IT Rules, 2021 and the identification of the "first originator" of a message. Rule 4(2) has been challenged as exceeding its parent provision and resting on no law made by Parliament, and that challenge is pending before the Delhi High Court. Raising it against a feature meant to share fewer identifiers fits a pattern. 

We ask MeitY to state the exact provision of law under which this notice, and the direction to halt the roll-out, has been issued, and to withdraw that direction. It should stop using Section 79 and the contested traceability rule as leverage to control product design and to reverse features that improve privacy. Impersonation and fraud are real risks, but they are met by enforcing the criminal law against those who commit them, and by open processes that rest on identified legal powers. They are not met by MeitY deciding, in private and by letter, what features Indians may use. That is a licence raj for software features.

New Delhi, 1 July 2026

https://t.co/X7ipfsWjp2 strongly objects to the arbitrary, unconstitutional takedown of online content deemed “objectionable, abusive, and offensive” by the Delhi Police today.

As reported, the Delhi Police's social media monitoring team has been scanning online platforms to identify objectionable content, and upon identification, has been sending notices to social media intermediaries directing them to remove the content. Both existing and newly uploaded content are being monitored, and at least three social media platforms have been served notices to take down content, subsequent to which, several posts have already been taken down.

This takedown drive is contrary to the rule of law and to India’s constitutional commitment to freedom of speech under Article 19(1)(a). The restrictions on free speech laid out in Article 19(2) are specific, and do not include “objectionable, abusive, or offensive” speech as one of the legitimate grounds to block free speech. Taking down content on the vague grounds that it is “objectionable” also directly contradicts the judgment of Shreya Singhal v Union of India, which struck down Section 66A of the Information Technology Act, 2000 precisely because the usage of words like “grossly offensive” and “menacing character” were undefined and therefore vague, arbitrary and unreasonable.

The current practice of issuing vague orders that invoke generic grounds such as “objectionable” or “offensive” is inconsistent with the safeguards laid down in Shreya Singhal. The Supreme Court upheld Section 69A of the Information Technology Act, 2000 strictly because it required that blocking orders must be reasoned, necessary, and proportionate, and that such reasons must be recorded in writing to enable judicial review. In the present case, notices sent to social media intermediaries through the Sahyog Portal under Section 79(3)(b) of the IT Act and Rule 3(1)(d) of the IT Rules, 2021, leave users in the dark, with no recourse to meaningfully challenge takedowns and leave affected parties without legal redressal. The Sahyog Portal puts in place a parallel system to take down content online, without any of the safeguards present under Section 69A.

The opacity surrounding these takedowns goes against the strict requirements of accountability and record-keeping embedded in the Information Technology (Procedure and Safeguards for Blocking for Access of Information by Public) Rules, 2009. Instead, what we see emerging through these takedowns is a system of informal, decentralised censorship, where the government can direct content removals without transparency or oversight.

https://t.co/X7ipfsWjp2 has consistently emphasised the need for transparency and primacy of user rights in content moderation. The cumulative effect of current developments is the creation of a black-box censorship regime, where users are silenced without any transparency or accessible remedies.

In light of the above, https://t.co/X7ipfsWjp2 calls for the following:

1. Immediate disclosure of all takedown orders issued to platforms, including specific reasons and legal justifications.

2. Strict adherence to the procedural safeguards laid out under Section 69A and the 2009 Blocking Rules, which were upheld by the Supreme Court in Shreya Singhal.

3. Notices received by social media intermediaries to be sent to every user affected to ensure transparency.

4. Strengthening of independent oversight and appellate mechanisms to ensure that users can effectively challenge unlawful restrictions.

INDIA CRACKS DOWN ON AI & DEEP FAKE. BIG TECH PUT ON NOTCE

1. What has actually changed?

The Modi government amended the Information Technology (Intermediary Guidelines and Digital Media Ethics Code) Rules, 2021 on 10 February 2026 specifically to deal with synthetically generated information and deepfakes.
The framework covers deceptive AI-generated audio, visual and audio-visual material.
The idea is no longer simply: remove illegal content after somebody complains.

Platforms are now being pushed towards:
identification
labelling
metadata
verification
automated detection
rapid takedown
and greater accountability for allowing unlawful AI content to spread.

2. AI CONTENT HAS TO BE IDENTIFIABLE
This is probably the biggest structural change.
AI-generated/synthetically altered material covered by the rules has to be clearly identifiable as synthetic.
Platforms/services enabling generation or alteration of such content must ensure appropriate labels or traceable identifiers/metadata.
The objective is simple:
REAL CONTENT ≠ AI CONTENT
The viewer should not have to conduct a forensic investigation to figure out whether something was artificially generated.
Important nuance

Don't say “every piece of text written using AI anywhere on the internet must carry a label.”

MeitY's FAQ clarifies that the operative 2026 SGI definition primarily targets audio, visual and audio-visual information, not ordinary AI-generated written text.
A more accurate line for your video is:
“India has mandated identification and labelling requirements for covered AI-generated synthetic media, particularly deepfake audio, images and video.”

3. THE BIG NUMBER: 36 HOURS → 3 HOURS

Previously, once an intermediary received legally valid knowledge of unlawful material through the prescribed government/court process, the compliance window could be 36 hours.

That has now been cut to:

3 HOURS

That is a 91.7% reduction in response time.

So something capable of going viral nationally during an election, riot, communal incident, stock-market panic or national-security crisis can no longer theoretically remain online for a day and a half after a valid takedown direction.

The platform has only hours.

4. AND SOME COMPLAINT WINDOWS ARE EVEN SHORTER

The government says timelines for grievance redressal have also been compressed.

According to the PIB explanation:
certain complaints earlier subject to 72 hours can now require action within 36 hours

particularly sensitive categories that earlier had a 24-hour timeline can now require action within 2 hours

This specifically matters for areas such as:

impersonation

intimate imagery

nudity

deepfake abuse

other highly sensitive material.

5. BIG TECH CAN'T JUST WAIT FOR A COMPLAINT

This is another major change.

The government says intermediaries must deploy reasonable and appropriate technical measures, including automated tools or other mechanisms, against unlawful synthetically generated content.
That means platforms are increasingly being pushed from:
REACTIVE MODERATION
to
PROACTIVE DETECTION
For Significant Social Media Intermediaries, the framework explicitly envisages technical measures to identify prohibited content, including certain forms of:

rape-related material

child sexual abuse material

repeat prohibited content

unlawful synthetic content.

6. USERS MAY HAVE TO DECLARE AI CONTENT

The synthetic-media framework also places responsibility upstream.

Major platforms can be required to ask users uploading covered content whether it is synthetically generated and then use technical systems to check that declaration.

So theoretically:
User uploads video →
declares AI/not AI →
platform checks →
synthetic material gets labelled.

The earlier draft framework explicitly envisaged this declaration + technical-verification model.

7. WHY THE METADATA PART MATTERS

A visible watermark can be:

cropped,
blurred,
edited,
screen-recorded,

reposted.

Metadata/identifiers create another layer of traceability.

The government's objective is therefore not merely:

“PUT AI GENERATED IN THE CAPTION.”
It is building a system where synthetic content can carry technological indicators allowing platforms to recognise what it is.
That becomes especially useful once the same manipulated video is downloaded and re-uploaded across multiple platforms.
8. THE RULES TARGET DEEPFAKE IMPERSONATION DIRECTLY
Existing IT Rules already prohibit users from publishing material that:

impersonates another person

misleads users about the origin of a message

knowingly spreads patently false or misleading information

threatens public order

violates another applicable law.

AI does not create an exemption.

If AI is being used for impersonation, fraud, defamatory fabrication or other unlawful activity, existing criminal and cyber provisions can also apply.

9. BNS CAN ALSO COME INTO PLAY
The PIB release specifically points towards provisions of the Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita.
Depending upon what the deepfake is being used for, authorities could examine provisions relating to:
Section 319 — cheating by personation
Section 336 — forgery

Section 353 — false information/rumours capable of causing public mischief or fear

Section 111 — organised crime, where the factual circumstances justify it.

So there isn't necessarily a standalone offence called simply:

“making a deepfake.”

The legal consequence depends heavily upon what the deepfake does.

10. CHILD SEXUAL ABUSE DEEPFAKES GET SPECIAL ATTENTION
This is perhaps the least discussed but most important provision.
The amended framework explicitly covers harmful AI-generated material involving:
child sexual exploitation

non-consensual intimate imagery

impersonation

other prohibited synthetic material.

Platforms are expected to prevent such content and act rapidly when detected.

11. SOCIAL-MEDIA GIANTS HAVE EXTRA DUTIES

Platforms classified as Significant Social Media Intermediaries, broadly those crossing the prescribed Indian user threshold, face additional compliance obligations.

These include mechanisms involving:
automated detection
grievance officers
compliance officers

local points of contact

India-based compliance structures

periodic compliance reports

appeals processes

originator tracing in specified circumstances for messaging services.
So the rules are aimed not only at the person creating the deepfake.
They put a major compliance burden on the distribution network itself.
12. THE REAL STICK: SAFE HARBOUR
This is where it becomes serious for Meta, X, Google, Telegram and other intermediaries.
Section 79 of the IT Act provides intermediaries conditional protection from liability for third-party content.
But that protection depends upon complying with the law and prescribed due diligence.
The PIB release reiterates that failure to observe obligations under the IT Rules can result in the intermediary losing its Section 79 exemption, after which liability can arise under applicable law.

That makes the real equation:

Comply with due diligence → retain intermediary protection

Ignore statutory obligations → safe-harbour protection can be jeopardised

That is far more powerful than merely issuing a fine.

13. GOVERNMENT HAS BUILT A TAKEDOWN PIPELINE

There is now an increasingly integrated enforcement architecture:

Grievance Appellate Committees — GACs

Indian Cyber Crime Coordination Centre — I4C

SAHYOG Portal

National Cyber Crime Reporting Portal

police/cybercrime units

authorised State and Central Government agencies.

The SAHYOG system in particular enables centralised electronic communication of lawful content-removal notices to intermediaries.

14. INDIA IS ALSO BUILDING ITS OWN DEEPFAKE-DETECTION TECHNOLOGY

Under the IndiaAI Mission's Safe & Trusted AI pillar, government-backed work includes indigenous detection and governance technologies.
PIB identifies projects including:
Saakshya — multi-agent deepfake-detection framework developed by IIT Jodhpur and IIT Madras
AI Vishleshak — audio-visual forgery detection
IIT Kharagpur work on real-time voice deepfake detection.

So this is not purely a legal crackdown.

It is simultaneously a:

LEGAL + PLATFORM + TECHNOLOGICAL framework.

15. WHY THIS IS HAPPENING NOW

Generative AI has destroyed the old assumption that:
“Seeing is believing.”
Today one person can manufacture:

a politician announcing something he never said

a CEO apparently moving a stock

an Army officer issuing a fake warning

communal speeches

celebrity pornography

fake financial endorsements

fabricated battlefield footage

false evidence of violence
within minutes.
And the fake can reach millions before conventional fact-checking catches up.
Therefore the Indian approach is increasingly:
IDENTIFY → LABEL → DETECT → TRACE → REMOVE → PROSECUTE
rather than merely:
WAIT → RECEIVE COMPLAINT → INVESTIGATE.
THE BIG STORY FOR YOUR VIDEO

The headline isn't simply:

“Deepfakes must carry labels.”

The bigger story is that India is trying to change where responsibility lies.

Earlier, platforms could largely argue:

A user uploaded it; we are merely the intermediary.

The regulatory direction is increasingly:

If you operate the technology that generates, distributes or algorithmically amplifies synthetic content in India, you have duties to identify it, label it and respond rapidly when it becomes unlawful.

HOPE THAT HELPS

Three weeks ago, the Department of Telecommunications notified a set of new rules. Every entity operating communication infrastructure in India, be it mobile tower companies, cloud-based telecom network providers, internet exchange points, or satellite gateways, must now store all their data exclusively within the country. 🧵👇

India hasn't always had strict data localization rules. The earliest version of them was restricted to just government records, which couldn't be transferred outside the country. Old telecom regulations also barred the overseas transfer of subscriber accounting information specifically. Nobody was thinking about "data sovereignty" as a grand national project.

In 2011, the government notified the IT SPDI Rules. This established baseline consent and security practices for companies handling sensitive personal data, like passwords, financial information, biometrics, and medical records. The first big case of business data being subject to such a mandate came in 2015, when IRDAI required insurers to keep core insurance records strictly within Indian territory.

Twelve names were enough to justify rules that named nobody.

What got built on top of that list reached millions of people who were never named at all. 🧵👇

text:
Prof. Manoj Kumar Jha @manojkjhadu, your “Muffled Voices” poses a question India cannot afford to answer casually: what if democracy survives electorally, yet citizens gradually become afraid to speak? 

More unsettling still—what if nobody formally silences us because anticipated consequences teach us to silence ourselves?

🧵 FREEDOM OF EXPRESSION & DEMOCRACY’S FATE: THE CONSTITUTIONAL ANATOMY OF A “CHILLING EFFECT”

You begin where democracy actually begins—not with elections, but information.

Alexander Meiklejohn's democratic theory treated speech as indispensable to self-government: citizens cannot meaningfully govern unless they can hear, question and judge competing claims.

India constitutionalises that intuition through Article 19(1)(a).

But freedom is deliberately not absolute. Article 19(2) permits reasonable restrictions concerning sovereignty and integrity of India, State security, friendly relations with foreign States, public order, decency or morality, contempt of court, defamation and incitement to an offence.

The constitutional equation is therefore neither:

Speech > everything

nor

State > speech

but:

Liberty + narrowly justified restraint = constitutional democracy.

The Supreme Court has repeatedly stressed that restrictions cannot simply be invented beyond Article 19(2)'s enumerated grounds.

text:
India already possesses a constitutional compass.

Romesh Thappar (1950) located circulation of ideas near democracy's foundations.

Bennett Coleman (1972) protected press freedom against measures whose practical effect constrained circulation.

Indian Express Newspapers (1985) reaffirmed press freedom within Article 19(1)(a).

Shreya Singhal (2015) struck down IT Act Section 66A, powerfully distinguishing discussion, advocacy and incitement.

Subramanian Swamy (2016) nevertheless upheld criminal defamation—reminding absolutists that reputation also receives constitutional protection.

Anuradha Bhasin (2020) reaffirmed press freedom and subjected restrictions affecting internet-based expression to constitutional scrutiny, while discussing chilling effect.

The jurisprudential message is beautifully difficult:

Protect dissent without constitutionalising abuse; regulate harm without bureaucratising truth.

text:
Your @manojkjhadu concern over governmental “fact-checking” acquires special contemporary significance.

The Bombay High Court struck down the 2023 IT Rules amendment enabling a Central Government Fact Check Unit concerning information about Central Government business, finding constitutional defects including vagueness and restrictions beyond Article 19(2).

But the story is not finished.

As of 20 August 2026, the Union's appeal is alive before the Supreme Court. 

In March 2026, the Court issued notice, declined to stay the Bombay High Court judgment and indicated that significant constitutional questions concerning misinformation require consideration.

That makes Jha's question remarkably current:

Can Government legitimately combat misinformation concerning itself without becoming simultaneously interested party, complainant and arbiter of truth?

Equally:

Can constitutional democracy simply abandon the information ecosystem to commercially incentivised misinformation?

Neither extreme solves the problem.

Independent process, statutory precision, transparency, proportionality and judicial review offer the more defensible middle path.

text:
🛑 LEGAL NOTICE

To,  

Mr. Kunal Kamra
Comedian
X Handle: @kunalkamra88

Subject: Legal Notice for Immediate Removal of Derogatory Video, Public Apology, and Cessation of Further Acts Outraging Hindu Religious Sentiments, Failing Which Legal Proceedings Shall Be Initiated.

Mr. Kunal,

1. You have, on or around 15 July 2026, during a protest/event organised by the “Cockroach Janta Party” at Jantar Mantar, Delhi, made and circulated a highly offensive, derogatory, and blasphemous statement in a video speech. 

2. In the said video (also uploaded/covered by HNP News at https://t.co/mdQV2ex1dP), you deliberately uttered words to the effect: “Sita ke pati ka naam le lekar Nita ke pati ka kaam kar rahe hain” (and elaborated in a similar mocking and irreverent tone). 

3. Here, “Sita ke pati” refers to Bhagwan Shri Ram and is used in conjunction with “Nita ke pati” (referring to a corporate figure). You thereby reduce the sacred names and divine personas of Bhagwan Shri Ram and Maa Sita, revered Deities central to Hindu faith, Dharma, and the religious beliefs of millions of Hindus, to mere tools for crude political commentary and sensationalism. 

4. The tone, context, and delivery clearly demonstrate mockery and contempt. Screenshots of the video are annexed for your reference.

5. You may criticise the Government on any issue you want, but using the sacred names of our Deities in such a manner cannot be allowed. You are expected to refrain from using the sacred names of our Deities in such a manner.

6. You are a comedian and public figure. While you have the right to criticise the policies or actions of the Government of India (which I and many others do not object to), you have absolutely no right to use the names of our sacred Deities casually, mock them, or make fun of them for the sake of cheap laughs, political point-scoring, or sensationalism. This is not satire, it is a deliberate insult to the religious beliefs and sentiments of millions of Hindus.

7. Comments on the video and across social media by thousands of Hindus clearly show that the religious sentiments of thousands of Hindus, including me, have been deeply hurt.

8. Your actions squarely attract the offences punishable under:  
- Section 299 BNS (Deliberate and malicious acts intended to outrage religious feelings)  
- Section 196/197 BNS (Promoting enmity between different groups on grounds of religion / Defamation)  
and other relevant provisions, r/w provisions of the Information Technology Act, 2000.

9. You are hereby called upon to take note of the Hon’ble Supreme Court’s binding Order dated 28.04.2023 passed in Ashwini Kumar Upadhyay vs. Union of India (W.P.(C) No.943/2021), wherein the Apex Court has directed all States/UTs to register suo moto FIRs against acts that outrage religious feelings, without waiting for any formal complaint, irrespective of the religion or status of the offender. Failure to act by authorities shall amount to contempt of the Supreme Court.

DEMANDS:

You are hereby directed to:
a) Immediately delete the offending video, all its copies, and related posts from all digital platforms within 48 hours of receipt/notice of this Legal Notice.
b) Issue a public unconditional apology on your X handle @kunalkamra88 (and other prominent platforms) for hurting the religious sentiments of Hindus by misusing the names of Bhagwan Shri Ram and Maa Sita.
c) Undertake in writing that you shall refrain from any further acts of using sacred Hindu Deities’ names casually or in a mocking/derogatory manner.

Since you yourself talk about morality and shame in your statement, we expect the same standards from you. 

We urge you to take back your words on Bhagwan Ram and Sita Mata and tender a public apology.

Please take notice that in case you fail to comply with the above demands within the stipulated time, I shall be constrained to:  

* Initiate appropriate criminal proceedings against you before the competent Court of law;  

* File complaints before the Police for registration of FIR as per the Supreme Court directions; and  

* Take all other legal remedies available to me under the law, including civil suit for damages.

This notice is sent to you without prejudice to my rights and contentions.

Amita Sachdeva
Advocate-on-Record
Supreme Court of India

hitting our $1.2M ARR wasn't about going viral or huge ad spend.

it was boring, tiny site tweaks most people miss.

here are the 8 steps & prompts that boosted your traffic and conversions:

0. Understand the Full System

website optimization isn’t just about changing the design.

it comes down to three stages:

① build a foundation Google and AI can crawl and understand
② attract visitors with useful content
③ use data to turn those visitors into signups and purchases

ranking on Google isn’t enough.

if AI engines can’t understand your content—or visitors land on your site but don’t understand the value—you still won’t get results.

the key is identifying which stage is broken and improving it with a clear goal.

if you want to improve your website or grow your organic traffic, bookmark this.

1. Understand What’s Happening With Data

the first step is making sure you can see what is actually happening.

not guesses. real data.

the two main tools you need are Google Analytics 4 (GA4) and Google Search Console (GSC).

both are free.

GA4 shows what people do after they visit your website:

・which pages get the most traffic
・whether visitors come from Google, social media, or other channels
・whether visitors come from AI tools like ChatGPT or Perplexity
・which pages lead to signups or purchases

Google Search Console shows how people discover you through Google:

・which keywords your pages appear for
・how many people click from search results
・your average search position
・which articles are gaining or losing rankings

with these two tools, you can separate two very different problems:

“not enough people are visiting”

vs.

“people are visiting, but they aren’t taking action”

connect GA4 and Google Search Console to NoimosAI, and it can analyze the data and suggest what to improve.

feed these prompts into NoimosAI to identify the room for improvement:
“Analyze traffic from Google Search and AI search engines using GA4 and GSC, then recommend the pages with the highest improvement potential.”

“Using GSC data, identify articles that have lost rankings and recommend which ones should be rewritten.”

2. Build a Technical Foundation Google and AI Can Understand

you can create the most useful content in your industry.

but if Google and AI can’t properly crawl and understand it, people won’t find it through search results or AI-generated answers.

here’s what to check:

・are your important pages indexed by Google?
・does your sitemap tell crawlers which pages exist?
・is robots.txt accidentally blocking Google or AI crawlers?
・does the site load quickly and work well on mobile?
・are there broken links or layout issues?
・does JSON-LD clearly identify your company, products, and articles?
・does llms.txt organize your most important pages for AI?

robots.txt, sitemaps, and JSON-LD create a shared technical foundation for both traditional search and AI search.

the work that helps Google discover and understand your pages is called technical SEO.

GEO goes one step further by making your content easier for AI engines to understand and use in their answers.

NoimosAI can analyze page speed, site structure, robots.txt, JSON-LD, and other technical issues—then recommend improvements for both search engines and AI.

use this prompt in NoimosAI to optimize your site:
“Audit [Website URL] for search engine and AI readability. Analyze robots.txt, the sitemap, JSON-LD, llms.txt, and page speed, then recommend specific improvements.”

3. Communicate Your Value Above the Fold

visitors decide within seconds whether they want to keep reading.

the first screen they see should answer three questions:

・who is this for?
・what problem does it solve?
・what should I do next?

listing dozens of features won’t help if visitors can’t see why the product matters to them.

for example, describing NoimosAI as “a powerful AI agent” is too abstract.

“delegate your marketing work to AI” makes the outcome much easier to understand.

don’t just describe the product.

show people what changes after they use it.

prompt to find the best messages for your site:
“Analyze the first screen visitors see on [Website URL], then suggest a headline and supporting copy that communicate the value immediately.”

4. Give People a Reason to Trust You and Take Action

interest alone doesn’t create signups.

even when people understand your service, they may still wonder:

“does this actually work?”

“will this work for my company?”

your website needs to answer those questions with evidence.

use things like:

・real product screenshots
・specific use cases
・customer results
・testimonials
・supported integrations
・security information
・pricing and the steps required to get started

don’t add everything just to make the page longer.

choose the proof that addresses the biggest concerns customers have before signing up.

on the NoimosAI website, we show the product, supported services, customer testimonials, and security information before guiding visitors toward getting started.

5. Choose Keywords That Can Generate Revenue

once the foundation is ready, you need to attract the right visitors.

a better website won’t generate results if nobody sees it.

start with the problems your customers are already searching for on Google.

then create articles that solve those problems and introduce your product as one possible solution.

the key: don’t target a keyword just because it has high search volume.

for example, “best AI tools” may get a lot of searches, but it is extremely competitive.

more specific keywords like:

“best AI tools for social media posts”

or:

“best AI tools for competitor analysis”

usually have clearer intent and less competition.

use data from Semrush or similar tools to find keywords that:

・match a real problem your customers have
・have enough search volume to matter
・aren’t dominated by impossible competition
・show comparison, evaluation, or purchase intent

a good keyword doesn’t just generate traffic.

it attracts people who could eventually become customers.

use this prompt to find the best keywords to get visitors:
“Find keywords that customers of [Product or Service] are searching for. Organize them by search volume, ranking difficulty, and search intent.”

6. Create Articles That Rank on Google and Get Understood by AI

once you choose a keyword, analyze the pages already ranking for it.

top-ranking pages reveal what people are expecting to find.

but copying the same information gives people no reason to read your article.

first, analyze the SEO side:

・what topics appear across most top-ranking articles?
・what order makes the information easiest to understand?
・what information is missing?
・what information is outdated?
・where can you add your own experience or data?

then make the structure easy for AI to understand:

・answer one clear question under each heading
・give the direct answer first
・summarize the most important points
・include examples, numbers, and sources
・add an FAQ at the end

don’t write an FAQ that avoids the question.

answer it directly in the first one or two sentences, then explain the reasoning and examples.

this makes the article easier for readers to scan and easier for AI to extract useful answers from.

that’s a core part of GEO.

NoimosAI can analyze Google search results, create the article structure, write the content, and include summaries, direct answers, and FAQs designed for both SEO and GEO.

prompt:
“Analyze the top-ranking search results for [Keyword], then create an SEO/GEO-optimized article targeting that keyword.”

7. Use Data to Find What to Improve

publishing a page is not the finish line.

algorithms change. information becomes outdated. customer behavior changes.

you need to keep improving based on what the data tells you.

the same “underperforming page” can have completely different problems:

・high search impressions, but few clicks
　→ the title or description isn’t compelling enough

・high rankings, but little traffic
　→ the keyword may have low search demand

・high traffic, but few signups
　→ the content, CTA, page flow, or trust signals may be weak

・an article used to perform, but rankings dropped
　→ the information may be outdated, or competitors may now offer better content

don’t try to fix every page at once.

identify the cause, then start with the pages where a small improvement could create the biggest result.

prompt to use in NoimosAI:
“Using GSC and GA4, categorize pages into: ① pages that don’t appear in search, ② pages that appear but don’t get clicked, and ③ pages that get traffic but don’t generate signups. Recommend improvements for each.”

8. Compare Before and After, Then Keep Improving

website optimization is never a one-time project.

when you change a title, check the click-through rate.

when you update an article, check its search ranking.

when you change the page structure, check the signup rate.

record every change and compare the numbers before and after.

that’s how you learn which improvements are actually driving results.

here’s what we review every month:

・pages gaining or losing search impressions
・pages gaining or losing traffic from ChatGPT, Perplexity, and other AI services
・pages with low click-through rates
・articles losing rankings
・high-traffic pages that don’t generate signups
・pages with speed issues
・traffic sources generating signups or purchases

we use NoimosAI agents to continuously identify keyword gaps and rewrite underperforming content.

feed these prompts into NoimosAI to find the gap between you and your competitors:
“Every week, identify high-priority keywords that competitors rank for but we don’t, then create one new article idea.”

“Every month, compare the latest 28 days with the previous 28 days. Use search rankings, clicks, and traffic from AI services to identify the article with the highest improvement potential and create a rewrite plan.”

website optimization isn’t about launching a flashy redesign.

it’s about:

・building a system that measures results
・making your value easy to understand
・creating content around real customer problems
・improving continuously based on data

repeat this process, and your website stops being a static company brochure.

it becomes a system that consistently generates customers.

# India: Autocratic Risk Assessment — August 2026
*Using the High-Visibility Risk Framework | Primary-Evidence Grounded*

---

## Executive Summary

**Assessed Risk Level: MODERATE** (with specific elevated sub-indicators)

India as of mid-to-late August 2026 does not meet the threshold for "high" risk of autocratic consolidation, but several risk indicators are active and reinforcing. The overall picture is one of a competitive, contested, and occasionally turbulent democracy under measurable strain — where balancing mechanisms are still functioning but are being partially eroded or contested in ways that warrant close monitoring.

**Key quantified highlights:**

- **Coalition arithmetic (protective):** The NDA holds approximately **293–319 seats** in the Lok Sabha (effective strength 540 seats; simple majority = 271). Constitutional amendments require a two-thirds supermajority of **360 votes**. The NDA falls **12–67 seats short** of that threshold depending on issue-based support. Even under the most favourable scenario (rebel TMC, Shiv Sena UBT, and DMK support), the alliance reaches approximately **346–348 votes** — still short. [2][3] In the Rajya Sabha (effective 242 seats, supermajority = 163), the NDA stands at approximately **141–151 effective votes**, also short. [3] **Confidence: High.** This is publicly reported, numerically consistent parliamentary arithmetic. Unilateral constitutional change remains arithmetically blocked as of this date.

- **CJP protests and response (mixed):** The May–July 2026 Cockroach Janta Party (CJP) youth protests — triggered by the National Testing Agency exam paper leak affecting ~2 million students — produced both risk indicators and protective responses simultaneously. Hundreds of minors were arrested; pellet guns and tear gas were used; AI-powered surveillance of protesters was alleged; FIRs were filed against social media critics of the Prime Minister. [1] These are elevated-risk indicators. However: the Supreme Court ordered the release of all arrested under-18s; state BJP governments withdrew cases after judicial and public pressure; Education Minister Dharmendra Pradhan resigned (July 25); a reform task force was announced; and a public examinations amendment bill was introduced in parliament (July 27). [1][2][3] The concessions were real and measurable.

- **Electoral integrity (contested):** The Election Commission's appointment process remains legally disputed — the 2023 Act removing the Chief Justice of India from the selection committee is under active Supreme Court challenge (*Jaya Thakur v. Union of India*, 2024, hearings ongoing in 2026). Allegations of deletion of ~65 lakh voters from Bihar rolls, targeting minorities and opposition supporters, are before the Supreme Court. [4] **Confidence: Moderate** (allegations have prima facie judicial standing, but the court has not yet ruled on the merits).

- **Press freedom and narrative control (elevated concern):** Delhi Police filed FIRs against social media users for criticism of the PM, sought user identity data from X (formerly Twitter), and were documented noting Instagram handles of protesters. These are active, verifiable risk indicators. The government rejects accusations of surveillance overreach, stating it acts "only in the public interest." [1]

**Status of major contested claims:**
- Voter roll deletions in Bihar: Before the Supreme Court; unverified at the evidentiary level.
- AI surveillance of protesters: Alleged by activists, with a Delhi High Court petition filed; not yet adjudicated.
- Electoral Commission bias: Disputed; some credible institutional voices (former CEC S.Y. Quraishi) have publicly raised concerns. [3]

**Overall mapping:**
- *Risk indicators active:* Selective enforcement; shrinking space for online criticism; contested electoral institution independence; opaque surveillance.
- *Protective mechanisms active:* Judiciary intervening and producing concrete outcomes; coalition arithmetic blocking supermajority; real political concessions extracted through public pressure; competitive parliamentary opposition.

**Main residual uncertainties:** Pace of Rajya Sabha seat accumulation by NDA; outcomes of pending Supreme Court cases on EC appointments and voter rolls; whether FIRs against social media users are prosecuted or quietly dropped; whether surveillance infrastructure normalises after the protests recede.

---

## 1. Institutional Independence and Electoral Processes

### Election Commission

The 2023 Chief Election Commissioner Act replaced an appointment mechanism that included the Chief Justice of India with one where the PM, a Union Cabinet Minister, and the Leader of Opposition form the selection committee — giving the ruling party a structural 2:1 vote majority on the panel. [4] The Supreme Court's 2023 Anoop Baranwal judgment had recommended the CJI's inclusion; the Act effectively reversed that. The *Jaya Thakur* challenge is still pending as of mid-2026, with no final ruling issued. [4]

**Former CEC S.Y. Quraishi** (writing in the Indian Express, published August 10, 2026) publicly stated that the EC "must consciously maintain an arm's-length relationship with the executive" and that "any perception of a cosy relationship… is antithetical to the constitutional scheme." He noted 23 Opposition parties wrote to the Chief Justice over electoral roll handling. [3] This is a significant credibility signal — a former head of the institution raising institutional concern.

**Voter roll integrity:** Allegations of ~65 lakh (6.5 million) voter deletions in Bihar, disproportionately targeting minorities and opposition supporters, are before the Supreme Court under a petition challenging the Special Intensive Revision (SIR) process. [4] The court has accepted the petition for hearing — indicating prima facie seriousness — but no evidentiary ruling has been delivered.

| Indicator | Status | Risk level |
|---|---|---|
| EC appointment mechanism | Executive-dominant; under SC challenge | Elevated |
| Voter roll integrity claims | Before SC; unverified on merits | Moderate–Elevated |
| Competitive elections still occurring | Yes — Bihar, Maharashtra elections held with losses for ruling side recorded historically | Protective |

**Confidence: Moderate.** The structural concern is well-documented (legally). Evidentiary proof of actual manipulation remains sub judice.

### Judiciary

The Supreme Court's conduct during the CJP crisis provides the clearest current evidence of **functional judicial independence**: it ordered release of minors, directed preservation of drone/CCTV footage of police action, directed that protesters' data not be made public, and took suo motu cognizance of excess force allegations. [1] This is not consistent with a fully captured judiciary. However, the pace and pattern of cases involving the executive in other domains (e.g., electoral law challenges) proceeds slowly, which some legal observers flag as selective institutional responsiveness.

**Confidence: Moderate-High** that the Supreme Court retains meaningful independence on high-visibility cases. Lower confidence on whether that extends uniformly to lower-visibility executive actions.

---

## 2. Enforcement and Crisis-Power Use

### CJP Protest Response — Timeline and Assessment

| Date | Action | Risk / Protective |
|---|---|---|
| Late June 2026 | Exam paper leak; protests begin | Neutral trigger |
| July (various) | Hundreds arrested including minors; pellet guns and tear gas used; AK-47 fired in air (officer later suspended) | **Risk** |
| July 23 | Modi's first public comment; fast-track courts announced | Partially protective |
| July 25 | Education Minister Pradhan resigns | **Protective** — genuine accountability |
| July 25–27 | BJP state governments withdraw cases in Bihar, Assam, Delhi, Maharashtra, West Bengal | **Protective** — responsive to pressure |
| July 26–27 | Nilekani task force; Public Examinations Amendment Bill introduced in parliament | **Protective** |
| July 29+ | FIRs against social media critics; X asked for user identity data; Instagram handles noted by police | **Risk** |
| July 29 | SC orders release of all under-18s; directs footage preservation | **Protective** — judicial check |

**Key asymmetry:** The government's initial response was coercive (arrests of minors, weapons use, surveillance). The concessions were real but came **after** judicial intervention and mass public pressure — not proactively or transparently. The post-protest continuation of FIRs against online critics, while the minister's resignation stands as a concession, suggests a bifurcated strategy: yield on high-visibility demands while continuing low-visibility enforcement against individuals.

**Alternative Interpretation A (more benign):** The government faced a genuine administrative failure (exam leaks), responded with excess police force that was later corrected via courts and political accountability, and the minister's resignation reflects a functioning political accountability mechanism in a democracy. The social media FIRs are routine law enforcement against what the government genuinely characterises as defamatory content.

**Alternative Interpretation B (more concerning):** The initial coercive response — including AI surveillance, noting of social media handles, and charging of minors — represents a deliberate deterrence strategy designed to raise the cost of dissent. Concessions were made only when the political cost of not making them became higher (BJP core voter base affected; election cycle pressures). The continuation of social media enforcement after the visible protest ended suggests the deterrence goal persisted.

**Which does the evidence support more strongly?** Neither interpretation is fully excludable. The evidence of **real concessions extracted through real public pressure** weighs toward Interpretation A on the specific protest outcome. But the **surveillance infrastructure deployment** and **post-protest FIR continuation** give Interpretation B meaningful evidentiary support. The two dynamics coexist: India demonstrates both competitive democratic responsiveness and an expanding low-visibility enforcement posture.

**Confidence: Moderate.**

---

## 3. Transparency and Narrative Control

**Active risk indicators identified:**

1. **Social media surveillance:** Police documentation of protesters' Instagram handles at the protest site; FIR filed demanding X provide full user identity, login/logout timestamps of critics of the PM. [1] These are primary-source documented actions.

2. **AI-powered surveillance allegations:** Activist Aishe Ghosh filed a Delhi High Court petition describing mass AI surveillance of protesters and seeking destruction of collected data. [1] This remains unverified at the evidentiary level (petition filed, not adjudicated).

3. **Narrative framing by government:** Defence Minister Rajnath Singh described protesters as "political tools" of the opposition. The Education Minister's resignation statement cited "anti-national forces." [2] This framing applies delegitimising labels to citizens engaged in non-violent, issue-based contestation — a risk indicator under the framework.

4. **Government's stated counter-position:** Officials state they act "only in the public interest" on platform regulation and enforcement. The PM's July 23 post on X addressed exam leaks directly, showing some form of public accountability. [1][2]

**Missing data:** There is no publicly available transparency report from the Indian government on the number of content takedown requests, user data requests to platforms, or the outcomes of FIRs against social media users in 2026. This is a significant evidentiary gap.

---

## 4. Protective Mechanisms Still Functioning

The framework requires equal assessment of balancing indicators. The following are clearly operative:

1. **Coalition arithmetic blocks unilateral constitutional change.** NDA is 12–67 seats short of the supermajority threshold in the Lok Sabha and approximately 12 short in the Rajya Sabha. [2][3] Constitutional amendments remain arithmetically dependent on opposition or independent support.

2. **Judiciary produced concrete, enforceable outcomes** against executive enforcement (minor releases, footage preservation orders). [1]

3. **Ministerial accountability functioned:** A cabinet minister resigned in direct response to public protest — described by Reuters as "the worst political crisis of Modi's third term." [3] This is a meaningful protective signal.

4. **Opposition is active and vocal:** Parliamentary disruptions in support of protesters occurred (July 22); opposition parties are pursuing court challenges on electoral rolls and EC appointments. [4]

5. **Civil society and press are functioning** — Al Jazeera, BBC, Reuters, and Indian outlets reported extensively and critically on state force; activist petitions were accepted by courts; a former CEC published institutional criticism in a major national newspaper (August 10, 2026). [1][2][3]

6. **Competitive elections still produce real losses:** Bihar and state-level elections have historically produced results adverse to the ruling alliance; the numerical data on NDA's arithmetic shortfall reflects a competitive political landscape.

---

## 5. Alternative Interpretations — Summary Matrix

| Evidence item | Interpretation A (less concerning) | Interpretation B (more concerning) | Better supported by |
|---|---|---|---|
| Minors arrested, then released after SC order | Enforcement error corrected via functioning courts | Deliberate overreach; courts as a safety valve that prevents political cost without changing posture | Mixed — both partially supported |
| Education minister resigned | Genuine democratic accountability | Strategic sacrifice to preserve core voter base and deflect systemic scrutiny | Interpretation A slightly stronger — resignation was real and precedent-setting |
| Social media FIRs post-protest | Routine defamation enforcement | Low-visibility continuation of deterrence strategy | Interpretation B — timing and targeting are notably political |
| EC appointment reform | Legitimate legislative reform of selection process | Structural weakening of electoral independence | Interpretation B — removing CJI from panel weakens independence structurally, regardless of intent |
| Voter roll deletions in Bihar | Routine revision process with procedural errors | Targeted disenfranchisement | Unresolved — sub judice |
| NDA arithmetic shortfall | Opposition remains arithmetically capable of blocking | NDA is accumulating strength toward supermajority at pace | Both — trajectory warrants monitoring |

---

## 6. Confidence Levels and Data Gaps

| Claim | Confidence | Key gap |
|---|---|---|
| NDA seat arithmetic | **High** | Seat changes from by-elections not fully resolved |
| CJP arrests and concessions | **High** | Exact number of still-active FIRs against protesters unknown |
| Ministerial resignation as genuine concession | **High** | — |
| AI surveillance deployment | **Low–Moderate** | Petition filed; no evidentiary ruling; no government transparency report |
| Bihar voter roll deletions | **Low** | Sub judice; no independent audit published |
| EC appointment process structural bias | **High** (structural) | Whether it produces biased operational outcomes: **Low** |
| Judiciary independence | **Moderate–High** | High-visibility cases show independence; lower-visibility cases under-documented |

**What primary data would most improve this assessment:**
1. A published, timestamped register of all FIRs filed against CJP protesters and their current status (withdrawn / active / convicted).
2. An independent audit of Bihar voter rolls before and after SIR, with demographic breakdown — this is the single highest-impact data gap.
3. The Supreme Court's eventual ruling in *Jaya Thakur v. Union of India* on EC appointment constitutionality.
4. Platform transparency reports from X and Meta on Indian government takedown/user-data requests in 2026.
5. A published, public rationale and time-bound mandate for any AI surveillance infrastructure deployed during the protests.

---

## Final Assessment

India in August 2026 sits at **MODERATE** overall risk, with **elevated** sub-indicators in three specific domains: (a) electoral institution independence, (b) online/social media enforcement posture, and (c) the trajectory of coalition arithmetic toward the supermajority threshold.

The clearest finding is a **dual dynamic**: visible, high-profile accountability mechanisms (courts, parliament, public pressure, press) remain operational and produced concrete outcomes during the CJP crisis — this is meaningful. Simultaneously, a pattern of low-visibility enforcement (social media surveillance, platform data requests, AI-tracking allegations) appears to be expanding, and its full scope remains opaque to public scrutiny. The framework's "core operating test" — that significant power use be "externally observable, time-bound where possible, and open to repeated public justification" — is being met selectively: met for high-visibility concessions, partially unmet for enforcement infrastructure.

No evidence currently supports the conclusion that India has crossed into autocratic consolidation. The evidence does support the conclusion that **specific risk vectors are active and should be monitored with primary-source rigour**, particularly electoral institution integrity, the pace of NDA's Rajya Sabha accumulation, and the normalisation of low-visibility digital enforcement.

*STATEMENT: Escalating Digital Censorship in India*

*New Delhi, February 28, 2026*

The Internet Freedom Foundation (IFF) is concerned by a cluster of online blocking and takedown actions and ISP level service disruptions reported between 24–28 February 2026. Across these incidents, users and affected services face restrictions without clear, timely reasons and without access to the underlying orders needed to challenge state action by exercising their rights to obtain legal remedy.

Developers reported severe, uneven disruption in access to Supabase across multiple Indian networks. Reporting indicates the disruption followed a government direction, with accounts suggesting use of Section 69A of the Information Technology Act, 2000. Yet there has been no public statement of the grounds, scope, or duration, and no accessible order for those impacted. Supabase has publicly stated that its domains became inaccessible due to a “ministry order”, and users have been pushed to workarounds such as alternative DNS or VPNs. In parallel, users on X (formerly Twitter) continue to receive “withheld in India” notices restricting specific posts within the country. Such notices usually do not provide the government order or its reasoning. Hence, for those who are being censored the basics of natural justice of a notice, opportunity for a hearing and remedy are delayed or absent.

This is enabled by secrecy built into the blocking framework. Section 69A is implemented through the 2009 Blocking Rules, which contemplate a committee process and, where feasible, notice to intermediaries and identifiable originators. But they also impose “strict confidentiality” over requests and actions taken. When orders and reasons are secret by default, affected persons cannot test legality, necessity, proportionality, or factual errors except through protracted litigation. When in _Shreya Singhal v. Union of India_ (2015), the Supreme Court upheld Section 69A while relying on the existence of procedural safeguards and reasoned decisions, indicating that impacted users could approach court in writ remedies. However, due to the operational secrecy and providing copies of orders and notices those who are censored and prevented from obtaining judicial remedy.

The February 2026 amendments to the IT Rules, 2021 further increase these risks. The substituted Rule 3(1)(d) requires intermediaries to remove or disable access within three hours of receiving “actual knowledge”, which can arise from a court order or a written “reasoned intimation” by authorised government officers. While the rule lists what a “reasoned intimation” should contain, the legal basis, statutory provision, nature of the unlawful act, and specific URL/identifier, the three-hour window pressures platforms to comply promptly which may often occur without any substantive assessment. These inherently opaque censorship practices are being accelerated through "Sahyog" portal. Developed by the Indian Cybercrime Coordination Centre (I4C), the Sahyog portal operates entirely without statutory footing, only being anchored in the IT Rules, 2021 that are created by executive notification. It functions as a censorship clearinghouse that deliberately bypasses the established, albeit weak, procedural safeguards of Section 69A. By routing automated takedown directives directly to intermediaries under Section 79(3)(b) of the IT Act, the portal structurally excludes citizens and impacted users from the grievance process.

We demand that the government introduce strictly judicially enforceable transparency requirements, publish all blocking orders, and restore the principles of natural justice to India's platform governance framework. Based on requests from our community we will also next week launch a rough public sheet in which social media users can input and add information on digital censorship.
