Statement : Shutting down Telegram is a band aid solution and is a disproportionate answer to exam fraud

The Internet Freedom Foundation objects to the directions announced today in the National Testing Agency's press release on action against the Telegram platform. On the NTA's recommendation, the Ministry of Electronics and Information Technology has, under Section 69A of the Information Technology Act, 2000, restricted access to the whole of Telegram in India until 22 June 2026, and has separately ordered the platform to switch off message-editing for every Indian user until 30 June 2026. This is a blunt, nationwide measure aimed at the conduct of rampant fraud rackets, and on the Government's own admission is constitutionally incompatible.

At the outset it is important to note that Section 69A and the Blocking Rules of 2009 framed under it allow the Government to block access to specific “information” on a computer resource. They do not extend to switching off an entire intermediary, still less to ordering a company to redesign its product by removing a feature for a whole country. In Shreya Singhal v Union of India, the Supreme Court upheld Section 69A because it is narrow and hedged with procedural safeguards. Reading it to authorise shutting down a platform that lakhs use is an overbroad restriction by the NTAs own admission. For the message-editing direction the release identifies no source of power at all. If one exists, the order must say so.

The release argues against itself

A restriction on access has to be the least intrusive measure that achieves its aim as per the constitutional test of proportionality laid down in Justice K.S. Puttaswamy v. Union of India (2017) and applied in Anuradha Bhasin v. Union of India (2020). The NTA's own narration shows the block fails its nodal agency, the release says, “has secured the prompt take-down of a substantial number of Telegram channels, groups and bots”, and this targeted work “is the reason the harm caused by these rackets has been contained to the extent it has”. If channel level takedown contained the harm, the case for a blanket block collapses and hence the Government has reached for a heavier tool while conceding that a lighter one was working. The collateral cost sits on the record too as noted in the press release. The block, the NTA accepts, “affects lakhs of citizens who use the Telegram platform for legitimate personal, educational, professional and informational purposes”. The release also says there is "no such paper available outside the secured examination chain" and that “the security of the examination is unaffected by the action taken”. If the exam is secure and no leak exists, what is being suppressed is rumour, and rumour cannot justify closing a platform when specific blocking and criminal prosecution remain available.

Students use of Telegram

The block of telegram is reactive and ineffective and will punish ordinary users instead of addressing the systemic source of exam leaks. This blocking comes in the final days of NEET preparation, when thousands of students depend on Telegram for study groups, doubt-clearing, and shared resources. Also, it is important to consider that the source of exam papers leak will occur from inside the system, among insiders and across the printing and logistics chain, with the platform being the most downstream channel for distribution. Hence, switching off Telegram, is merely a deflection from the repeated failures that will continue while media attention is directed towards this Telegram ban.

Lack of transparency

At present only a press release from the NTA has been provided, which recommended the block but the reasoned order of MeitY, the authority that issued it, has not been released. The Anuradha Bhasin decision requires that orders restricting access be published so they can be tested in court. Here the order, and the reasoning of the committee behind it, stay out of view, and we do not know whether Telegram was heard at all. An announcement of a block is no substitute for an order the affected party can challenge.
Blunt to enforce and very easy to evade
Usually, app-level blocks run through IS-level DNS and IP filtering. They are over inclusive, sweeping in lawful use, yet simple to evade as a determined exam leak racket moves to a VPN or a mirror within minutes while ordinary users lose the service for a week.

We ask the Government to:

1) Publish the MeitY Section 69A order and the NTA recommendation behind it, with reasons;
2) State the legal basis for the message editing direction, or withdraw it;
3) Confirm whether Telegram was given a hearing under the Blocking Rules, and place the committee's record before any court that hears a challenge; and
4) Lift the platform-wide restriction and rely on the targeted takedowns the NTA itself credits with containing the harm.

We emphasise that the NEET (UG) 2026 re-examination is worth protecting and it concerns the future of lakhs of aspirants. It requires securing the entire process of examination rather than reaching for purported band aid solutions that instead cause more harm. The State cannot switch off a service used by lakhs to answer the wrongdoing of a few, and cannot do it through an order no one affected is allowed to read. On its own facts, the Government has done both.

New Delhi, 16 June 2026.

*STATEMENT: Escalating Digital Censorship in India*

*New Delhi, February 28, 2026*

The Internet Freedom Foundation (IFF) is concerned by a cluster of online blocking and takedown actions and ISP level service disruptions reported between 24–28 February 2026. Across these incidents, users and affected services face restrictions without clear, timely reasons and without access to the underlying orders needed to challenge state action by exercising their rights to obtain legal remedy.

Developers reported severe, uneven disruption in access to Supabase across multiple Indian networks. Reporting indicates the disruption followed a government direction, with accounts suggesting use of Section 69A of the Information Technology Act, 2000. Yet there has been no public statement of the grounds, scope, or duration, and no accessible order for those impacted. Supabase has publicly stated that its domains became inaccessible due to a “ministry order”, and users have been pushed to workarounds such as alternative DNS or VPNs. In parallel, users on X (formerly Twitter) continue to receive “withheld in India” notices restricting specific posts within the country. Such notices usually do not provide the government order or its reasoning. Hence, for those who are being censored the basics of natural justice of a notice, opportunity for a hearing and remedy are delayed or absent.

This is enabled by secrecy built into the blocking framework. Section 69A is implemented through the 2009 Blocking Rules, which contemplate a committee process and, where feasible, notice to intermediaries and identifiable originators. But they also impose “strict confidentiality” over requests and actions taken. When orders and reasons are secret by default, affected persons cannot test legality, necessity, proportionality, or factual errors except through protracted litigation. When in _Shreya Singhal v. Union of India_ (2015), the Supreme Court upheld Section 69A while relying on the existence of procedural safeguards and reasoned decisions, indicating that impacted users could approach court in writ remedies. However, due to the operational secrecy and providing copies of orders and notices those who are censored and prevented from obtaining judicial remedy.

The February 2026 amendments to the IT Rules, 2021 further increase these risks. The substituted Rule 3(1)(d) requires intermediaries to remove or disable access within three hours of receiving “actual knowledge”, which can arise from a court order or a written “reasoned intimation” by authorised government officers. While the rule lists what a “reasoned intimation” should contain, the legal basis, statutory provision, nature of the unlawful act, and specific URL/identifier, the three-hour window pressures platforms to comply promptly which may often occur without any substantive assessment. These inherently opaque censorship practices are being accelerated through "Sahyog" portal. Developed by the Indian Cybercrime Coordination Centre (I4C), the Sahyog portal operates entirely without statutory footing, only being anchored in the IT Rules, 2021 that are created by executive notification. It functions as a censorship clearinghouse that deliberately bypasses the established, albeit weak, procedural safeguards of Section 69A. By routing automated takedown directives directly to intermediaries under Section 79(3)(b) of the IT Act, the portal structurally excludes citizens and impacted users from the grievance process.

We demand that the government introduce strictly judicially enforceable transparency requirements, publish all blocking orders, and restore the principles of natural justice to India's platform governance framework. Based on requests from our community we will also next week launch a rough public sheet in which social media users can input and add information on digital censorship.

INDIA’S NEXT CYBERCRIME RACE IS AGAINST THE STABLECOIN CLOCK

India's law-enforcement challenge is changing.

Earlier, when cybercrime money entered a mule bank account, investigators could identify the account, alert the bank and attempt to freeze the funds.

Today, the money can change form before the freeze reaches it.

₹ → Mule Account → P2P/OTC → USDT → Wallet → Multiple Wallets → Crypto Platforms

The bank account may be frozen.

But the value may already be somewhere else.

This is why stablecoins such as USDT deserve serious attention from India's law-enforcement and financial-intelligence ecosystem.

Stablecoins themselves are not illegal and have legitimate uses.

The risk comes from their combination of:

near-instant 24x7 transferability
dollar-linked value
global liquidity
P2P and OTC availability
unhosted/private wallets
offshore crypto platforms
movement across multiple blockchain networks
rapid conversion between fiat and crypto

FATF's March 2026 report highlighted the scale of the challenge: stablecoins accounted for an estimated 84% of the $154 billion illicit virtual-asset transaction volume identified for 2025.

India is already seeing the problem on the ground.

In July 2026, the Government of India disclosed an FIU-IND cyber-fraud case involving approximately ₹868 crore, more than 5,000 mule bank accounts and complex cryptocurrency transactions across multiple jurisdictions.

ED has separately reported investigations where cyber-fraud proceeds were converted into USDT through P2P transactions.

THIS CHANGES THE INVESTIGATION CLOCK.

A traditional financial investigation may ask:

"Which bank account received the money?"

A modern cybercrime investigation must immediately ask:

"Has the money already become crypto?"

"Which blockchain?"

"Which token?"

"Which wallet?"

"Which exchange or P2P counterparty?"

"Has it moved offshore?"

"Can it still be frozen?"

Tracing a blockchain transaction and recovering the asset are two completely different challenges.

For India, this requires the next generation of law-enforcement readiness:

24x7 crypto-response capability for cyber financial fraud.

Immediate capture of #wallet addresses, transaction hashes, blockchain/network and exchange information when a complaint is filed.

Real-time coordination between State Cyber Police, I4C, FIU-IND, ED, banks and VDA service providers.

Rapid preservation and lawful freezing requests to Indian and overseas exchanges.

Dedicated procedures for P2P, OTC, unhosted wallets, bridges and offshore VASPs.

Blockchain-forensics capability at State and district cybercrime units—not only at specialised central agencies.

Faster international cooperation when funds reach foreign platforms.

Clear operational protocols with stablecoin issuers and VASPs for lawful freezing, seizure and victim recovery.

India has already built important infrastructure. MHA's Sahyog Portal facilitates communication with VDA service providers, including data disclosure, asset freezing, tracking and transfer of seized assets pursuant to competent authority or court processes.

But technology moves in seconds.

Legal requests, institutional coordination and international assistance often do not.

That gap is where recovery can be lost.

The policy question is therefore no longer only:

"How do we regulate cryptocurrency?"

It is also:

"CAN INDIAN LAW ENFORCEMENT MOVE AS FAST AS DIGITAL VALUE?"

Stablecoins have changed the speed of financial crime.

India's investigative architecture must now change with it.

Statement : IFF condemns the internet shutdown in parts of Central Delhi. No suspension order has been made public.

New Delhi, 20 July 2026

The Internet Freedom Foundation (IFF) condemns the suspension of mobile internet services imposed today, 20 July 2026, in parts of Central Delhi, including the area around Jantar Mantar. The shutdown coincided with the 'Chalo Sansad' march called by the Cockroach Janta Party (CJP) on the opening day of the Monsoon Session of Parliament, where thousands of students and young people had gathered to press their demands. Permission for the march was refused. Prohibitory orders were imposed under Section 163 of the Bharatiya Nagarik Suraksha Sanhita, 2023. Routes to Parliament were sealed, and metro stations including, Patel Chowk, Rajiv Chowk and Janpath were closed. Amid reports of the use of force to disperse protesters, mobile internet was then switched off, reportedly "as a precautionary measure". We urge the immediate restoration of all telecommunication services in the capital and an end to internet shutdowns across India.

The developments of today are of immense consequence to the future of our democracy. The voices gathered at Jantar Mantar, and the residents of the national capital, need to be heard the loudest, not silenced en masse.

No order has been made public

At the time of release of this statement, no copy of any suspension order has been published by the Ministry of Home Affairs, the Department of Telecommunications, the Government of NCT of Delhi or the Delhi Police. Residents of the capital do not know which authority directed the shutdown, on what grounds, over which precise areas, for which services, or for what duration. An unpublished order is an unaccountable order. It cannot be challenged before a court, and the judicial review guaranteed by the Supreme Court becomes illusory. Some reports further indicate the deployment of network jammers in parts of Central Delhi, including near Jantar Mantar. Jamming equipment finds no sanction in the legal framework for the suspension of telecommunication services at all. If jammers were deployed, the government must disclose under what legal authority.

Binding safeguards violated

On 10 January 2020, the Supreme Court in Anuradha Bhasin v. Union of India, (2020) 3 SCC 637 held that the freedom of speech and expression, and the freedom to carry on trade or business through the medium of the internet, are protected under Articles 19(1)(a) and 19(1)(g) of the Constitution. The Court directed that every order suspending telecom services must be published. Reasons must be recorded in writing. The restriction must be proportionate, adopting the least restrictive measure available. It cannot continue indefinitely. It is subject to judicial review, and to scrutiny by a review committee.

Parliament has since replaced the framework of the Indian Telegraph Act, 1885. Under Section 20(2)(b) of the Telecommunications Act, 2023, telecommunication services may be suspended only on the occurrence of a public emergency or in the interest of public safety, on the grounds specified in that provision, and for reasons recorded in writing. The Telecommunications (Temporary Suspension of Services) Rules, 2024, notified on 22 November 2024, give effect to this power. A suspension order may be issued only by the Union Home Secretary or the State Home Secretary. An officer not below the rank of Joint Secretary may act in unavoidable circumstances, subject to confirmation by the competent authority within twenty four hours. Every order must clearly define the geographical area and the specific services suspended, and cannot remain in operation beyond fifteen days. Every order must also be published. A Review Committee must meet within five days of the order and record its findings on whether it complies with Section 20(2).

These safeguards are not being followed

If we account for today's shutdown against this legal architecture. The order is unpublished, in breach of Anuradha Bhasin and the Suspension Rules, 2024 alike. No recorded reasons are available to the public despite little to no reports of violence and consistent calls for the protest to be peaceful by the CJP and other organisers. The precise areas and services covered are undisclosed and so is the duration. Whether the competent authority even issued the order cannot be known. Whether the Review Committee will examine it cannot be verified. While the Suspension Rules prescribe no outer time limit for publication, a gap we have previously flagged, it cannot cut against the spirit of the Anuradha Bhasin judgement. A blanket suspension across densely populated parts of the capital, imposed as a "precaution" against a march to Parliament, is the opposite of a narrowly tailored, least restrictive measure. A shutdown timed to a protest restricts the freedoms of speech and assembly at the very moment they matter most.

The human cost of a shutdown

Access to the internet is a digital right on which the exercise of our fundamental freedoms now depends. When the network goes dark in Central Delhi, a journalist at Jantar Mantar cannot file her report or broadcast live. A street vendor on the surrounding roads cannot accept a UPI payment. A gig worker loses a day's earnings. A parent cannot confirm that a child who joined the march is safe. Cutting off communications prevents people from reaching out for help and manufactures panic in a moment which demands calm. These costs fall hardest on daily wage earners and small traders who can least absorb them. Internet based communications also promote trust between people and their government. 

A pattern, not an aberration

Delhi has seen this before. On 19 December 2019, mobile services were suspended for the first time in the capital's history during the protests against the Citizenship (Amendment) Act, in areas including Seelampur, Jamia Nagar and Mandi House. On 26 January 2021, the Ministry of Home Affairs suspended internet services in Singhu, Ghazipur, Tikri, Mukarba Chowk, Nangloi and their adjoining areas during the farmers' protests. According to the #KeepItOn coalition's report released in March 2026, India recorded 65 internet shutdowns in 2025, the highest of any democracy in the world, and accounts for 920 of the 2,102 shutdowns documented globally since 2016. We have consistently advocated against the harm these disruptions cause, from Jammu and Kashmir to Rajasthan, and from Haryana to Manipur, where a shutdown in 2023 ran for over two hundred days. The orders are rarely published on time, and the findings of review committees never see daylight.

Our demands

We call upon the Government of India and the Government of NCT of Delhi to:

1. Immediately restore all suspended telecommunication and internet services in Central Delhi.
2. Publish forthwith every suspension order passed on or around 20 July 2026, together with the reasons recorded in writing, as mandated by Anuradha Bhasin and the Telecommunications (Temporary Suspension of Services) Rules, 2024.
3. Disclose the issuing authority, the grounds, the precise areas and services covered, and the period of operation, and clarify whether network jammers were deployed and under what legal authority.
4. Place the order before the Review Committee within five days as required by the Rules, and make its findings public.
5. Reform Section 20(2)(b) of the Telecommunications Act, 2023 to provide for independent prior authorisation and real consequences for unlawful suspensions.

IFF will file applications under the Right to Information Act, 2005 seeking copies of the suspension orders and the records of the Review Committee, and is examining further legal remedies. 

Delhi and all of India deserve better.

Global Embarrassment

The government’s clumsy and ridiculous manner of “implementing” the Supreme Court’s order regarding Imran Khan’s health has brought disgrace and humiliation upon this government internationally.

The Supreme Court’s clear order was that Imran Khan should be taken to Shifa Hospital, where a medical board comprising Shifa’s doctors, in the presence of Imran’s personal physician and his sister, Dr. Uzma, would examine him, and that he would remain ostensibly there until September 16, when the court was to review the entire record.

At 12:23, Imran Khan was taken to PIMS Hospital, and at 5:00 he was declared healthy and sent back to jail.

This clearly demonstrates that the Shehbaz government was unwilling to comply with the Supreme Court’s order. Playing fast and loose with the law has long been the PML-N’s modus operandi—whether it was removing Junejo from the party presidency and creating the PML-N, the Memogate case, the attack on the judiciary, Nawaz Sharif’s platelet case, or the case of Imran Khan.

Had the government honestly implemented the Supreme Court’s decision, it would have deserved appreciation, political pressure would have eased, and an environment conducive to dialogue with the PTI would have emerged. But the PML-N leadership, blinded by its hatred for Imran Khan, appears determined to settle old scores.

Now condemnation is raining down from around the world.

And political tensions in the country will intensify further. So, whose bed will be rolled up next? Let us see. How long will the Field Marshal tolerate the stench of the hybrid system, when his office (CDSO) has, through an emergency amendment, been made autonomous from and superior to the Ministry of Defence, with sweeping powers?

It seems the Sharif Company has lost its bearings. It does not want PTI to settle its differences with the military. Yet Zulfi Bukhari, one of Imran Khan’s closest associates, welcomed the Supreme Court’s decision and had assured that there would be peaceful coexistence with the establishment.

Now the question is whether the Supreme Court will stand firm over its contempt, or whether the Shehbaz government will quietly retreat with its tail between its legs.

And if the PPP joins the Grand Opposition after the inclusion of Maulana Fazlur Rehman, who will save the PML-N’s lights from being extinguished, when the CDS office has become autonomous and beyond the Ministry of Defence, while the unemployed Defence Minister, Khawaja Asif, shamelessly sits outside the ministry’s door, crying over the same old grievances?

By Imtiaz Alam

# India: Autocratic Risk Assessment — August 2026
*Using the High-Visibility Risk Framework | Primary-Evidence Grounded*

---

## Executive Summary

**Assessed Risk Level: MODERATE** (with specific elevated sub-indicators)

India as of mid-to-late August 2026 does not meet the threshold for "high" risk of autocratic consolidation, but several risk indicators are active and reinforcing. The overall picture is one of a competitive, contested, and occasionally turbulent democracy under measurable strain — where balancing mechanisms are still functioning but are being partially eroded or contested in ways that warrant close monitoring.

**Key quantified highlights:**

- **Coalition arithmetic (protective):** The NDA holds approximately **293–319 seats** in the Lok Sabha (effective strength 540 seats; simple majority = 271). Constitutional amendments require a two-thirds supermajority of **360 votes**. The NDA falls **12–67 seats short** of that threshold depending on issue-based support. Even under the most favourable scenario (rebel TMC, Shiv Sena UBT, and DMK support), the alliance reaches approximately **346–348 votes** — still short. [2][3] In the Rajya Sabha (effective 242 seats, supermajority = 163), the NDA stands at approximately **141–151 effective votes**, also short. [3] **Confidence: High.** This is publicly reported, numerically consistent parliamentary arithmetic. Unilateral constitutional change remains arithmetically blocked as of this date.

- **CJP protests and response (mixed):** The May–July 2026 Cockroach Janta Party (CJP) youth protests — triggered by the National Testing Agency exam paper leak affecting ~2 million students — produced both risk indicators and protective responses simultaneously. Hundreds of minors were arrested; pellet guns and tear gas were used; AI-powered surveillance of protesters was alleged; FIRs were filed against social media critics of the Prime Minister. [1] These are elevated-risk indicators. However: the Supreme Court ordered the release of all arrested under-18s; state BJP governments withdrew cases after judicial and public pressure; Education Minister Dharmendra Pradhan resigned (July 25); a reform task force was announced; and a public examinations amendment bill was introduced in parliament (July 27). [1][2][3] The concessions were real and measurable.

- **Electoral integrity (contested):** The Election Commission's appointment process remains legally disputed — the 2023 Act removing the Chief Justice of India from the selection committee is under active Supreme Court challenge (*Jaya Thakur v. Union of India*, 2024, hearings ongoing in 2026). Allegations of deletion of ~65 lakh voters from Bihar rolls, targeting minorities and opposition supporters, are before the Supreme Court. [4] **Confidence: Moderate** (allegations have prima facie judicial standing, but the court has not yet ruled on the merits).

- **Press freedom and narrative control (elevated concern):** Delhi Police filed FIRs against social media users for criticism of the PM, sought user identity data from X (formerly Twitter), and were documented noting Instagram handles of protesters. These are active, verifiable risk indicators. The government rejects accusations of surveillance overreach, stating it acts "only in the public interest." [1]

**Status of major contested claims:**
- Voter roll deletions in Bihar: Before the Supreme Court; unverified at the evidentiary level.
- AI surveillance of protesters: Alleged by activists, with a Delhi High Court petition filed; not yet adjudicated.
- Electoral Commission bias: Disputed; some credible institutional voices (former CEC S.Y. Quraishi) have publicly raised concerns. [3]

**Overall mapping:**
- *Risk indicators active:* Selective enforcement; shrinking space for online criticism; contested electoral institution independence; opaque surveillance.
- *Protective mechanisms active:* Judiciary intervening and producing concrete outcomes; coalition arithmetic blocking supermajority; real political concessions extracted through public pressure; competitive parliamentary opposition.

**Main residual uncertainties:** Pace of Rajya Sabha seat accumulation by NDA; outcomes of pending Supreme Court cases on EC appointments and voter rolls; whether FIRs against social media users are prosecuted or quietly dropped; whether surveillance infrastructure normalises after the protests recede.

---

## 1. Institutional Independence and Electoral Processes

### Election Commission

The 2023 Chief Election Commissioner Act replaced an appointment mechanism that included the Chief Justice of India with one where the PM, a Union Cabinet Minister, and the Leader of Opposition form the selection committee — giving the ruling party a structural 2:1 vote majority on the panel. [4] The Supreme Court's 2023 Anoop Baranwal judgment had recommended the CJI's inclusion; the Act effectively reversed that. The *Jaya Thakur* challenge is still pending as of mid-2026, with no final ruling issued. [4]

**Former CEC S.Y. Quraishi** (writing in the Indian Express, published August 10, 2026) publicly stated that the EC "must consciously maintain an arm's-length relationship with the executive" and that "any perception of a cosy relationship… is antithetical to the constitutional scheme." He noted 23 Opposition parties wrote to the Chief Justice over electoral roll handling. [3] This is a significant credibility signal — a former head of the institution raising institutional concern.

**Voter roll integrity:** Allegations of ~65 lakh (6.5 million) voter deletions in Bihar, disproportionately targeting minorities and opposition supporters, are before the Supreme Court under a petition challenging the Special Intensive Revision (SIR) process. [4] The court has accepted the petition for hearing — indicating prima facie seriousness — but no evidentiary ruling has been delivered.

| Indicator | Status | Risk level |
|---|---|---|
| EC appointment mechanism | Executive-dominant; under SC challenge | Elevated |
| Voter roll integrity claims | Before SC; unverified on merits | Moderate–Elevated |
| Competitive elections still occurring | Yes — Bihar, Maharashtra elections held with losses for ruling side recorded historically | Protective |

**Confidence: Moderate.** The structural concern is well-documented (legally). Evidentiary proof of actual manipulation remains sub judice.

### Judiciary

The Supreme Court's conduct during the CJP crisis provides the clearest current evidence of **functional judicial independence**: it ordered release of minors, directed preservation of drone/CCTV footage of police action, directed that protesters' data not be made public, and took suo motu cognizance of excess force allegations. [1] This is not consistent with a fully captured judiciary. However, the pace and pattern of cases involving the executive in other domains (e.g., electoral law challenges) proceeds slowly, which some legal observers flag as selective institutional responsiveness.

**Confidence: Moderate-High** that the Supreme Court retains meaningful independence on high-visibility cases. Lower confidence on whether that extends uniformly to lower-visibility executive actions.

---

## 2. Enforcement and Crisis-Power Use

### CJP Protest Response — Timeline and Assessment

| Date | Action | Risk / Protective |
|---|---|---|
| Late June 2026 | Exam paper leak; protests begin | Neutral trigger |
| July (various) | Hundreds arrested including minors; pellet guns and tear gas used; AK-47 fired in air (officer later suspended) | **Risk** |
| July 23 | Modi's first public comment; fast-track courts announced | Partially protective |
| July 25 | Education Minister Pradhan resigns | **Protective** — genuine accountability |
| July 25–27 | BJP state governments withdraw cases in Bihar, Assam, Delhi, Maharashtra, West Bengal | **Protective** — responsive to pressure |
| July 26–27 | Nilekani task force; Public Examinations Amendment Bill introduced in parliament | **Protective** |
| July 29+ | FIRs against social media critics; X asked for user identity data; Instagram handles noted by police | **Risk** |
| July 29 | SC orders release of all under-18s; directs footage preservation | **Protective** — judicial check |

**Key asymmetry:** The government's initial response was coercive (arrests of minors, weapons use, surveillance). The concessions were real but came **after** judicial intervention and mass public pressure — not proactively or transparently. The post-protest continuation of FIRs against online critics, while the minister's resignation stands as a concession, suggests a bifurcated strategy: yield on high-visibility demands while continuing low-visibility enforcement against individuals.

**Alternative Interpretation A (more benign):** The government faced a genuine administrative failure (exam leaks), responded with excess police force that was later corrected via courts and political accountability, and the minister's resignation reflects a functioning political accountability mechanism in a democracy. The social media FIRs are routine law enforcement against what the government genuinely characterises as defamatory content.

**Alternative Interpretation B (more concerning):** The initial coercive response — including AI surveillance, noting of social media handles, and charging of minors — represents a deliberate deterrence strategy designed to raise the cost of dissent. Concessions were made only when the political cost of not making them became higher (BJP core voter base affected; election cycle pressures). The continuation of social media enforcement after the visible protest ended suggests the deterrence goal persisted.

**Which does the evidence support more strongly?** Neither interpretation is fully excludable. The evidence of **real concessions extracted through real public pressure** weighs toward Interpretation A on the specific protest outcome. But the **surveillance infrastructure deployment** and **post-protest FIR continuation** give Interpretation B meaningful evidentiary support. The two dynamics coexist: India demonstrates both competitive democratic responsiveness and an expanding low-visibility enforcement posture.

**Confidence: Moderate.**

---

## 3. Transparency and Narrative Control

**Active risk indicators identified:**

1. **Social media surveillance:** Police documentation of protesters' Instagram handles at the protest site; FIR filed demanding X provide full user identity, login/logout timestamps of critics of the PM. [1] These are primary-source documented actions.

2. **AI-powered surveillance allegations:** Activist Aishe Ghosh filed a Delhi High Court petition describing mass AI surveillance of protesters and seeking destruction of collected data. [1] This remains unverified at the evidentiary level (petition filed, not adjudicated).

3. **Narrative framing by government:** Defence Minister Rajnath Singh described protesters as "political tools" of the opposition. The Education Minister's resignation statement cited "anti-national forces." [2] This framing applies delegitimising labels to citizens engaged in non-violent, issue-based contestation — a risk indicator under the framework.

4. **Government's stated counter-position:** Officials state they act "only in the public interest" on platform regulation and enforcement. The PM's July 23 post on X addressed exam leaks directly, showing some form of public accountability. [1][2]

**Missing data:** There is no publicly available transparency report from the Indian government on the number of content takedown requests, user data requests to platforms, or the outcomes of FIRs against social media users in 2026. This is a significant evidentiary gap.

---

## 4. Protective Mechanisms Still Functioning

The framework requires equal assessment of balancing indicators. The following are clearly operative:

1. **Coalition arithmetic blocks unilateral constitutional change.** NDA is 12–67 seats short of the supermajority threshold in the Lok Sabha and approximately 12 short in the Rajya Sabha. [2][3] Constitutional amendments remain arithmetically dependent on opposition or independent support.

2. **Judiciary produced concrete, enforceable outcomes** against executive enforcement (minor releases, footage preservation orders). [1]

3. **Ministerial accountability functioned:** A cabinet minister resigned in direct response to public protest — described by Reuters as "the worst political crisis of Modi's third term." [3] This is a meaningful protective signal.

4. **Opposition is active and vocal:** Parliamentary disruptions in support of protesters occurred (July 22); opposition parties are pursuing court challenges on electoral rolls and EC appointments. [4]

5. **Civil society and press are functioning** — Al Jazeera, BBC, Reuters, and Indian outlets reported extensively and critically on state force; activist petitions were accepted by courts; a former CEC published institutional criticism in a major national newspaper (August 10, 2026). [1][2][3]

6. **Competitive elections still produce real losses:** Bihar and state-level elections have historically produced results adverse to the ruling alliance; the numerical data on NDA's arithmetic shortfall reflects a competitive political landscape.

---

## 5. Alternative Interpretations — Summary Matrix

| Evidence item | Interpretation A (less concerning) | Interpretation B (more concerning) | Better supported by |
|---|---|---|---|
| Minors arrested, then released after SC order | Enforcement error corrected via functioning courts | Deliberate overreach; courts as a safety valve that prevents political cost without changing posture | Mixed — both partially supported |
| Education minister resigned | Genuine democratic accountability | Strategic sacrifice to preserve core voter base and deflect systemic scrutiny | Interpretation A slightly stronger — resignation was real and precedent-setting |
| Social media FIRs post-protest | Routine defamation enforcement | Low-visibility continuation of deterrence strategy | Interpretation B — timing and targeting are notably political |
| EC appointment reform | Legitimate legislative reform of selection process | Structural weakening of electoral independence | Interpretation B — removing CJI from panel weakens independence structurally, regardless of intent |
| Voter roll deletions in Bihar | Routine revision process with procedural errors | Targeted disenfranchisement | Unresolved — sub judice |
| NDA arithmetic shortfall | Opposition remains arithmetically capable of blocking | NDA is accumulating strength toward supermajority at pace | Both — trajectory warrants monitoring |

---

## 6. Confidence Levels and Data Gaps

| Claim | Confidence | Key gap |
|---|---|---|
| NDA seat arithmetic | **High** | Seat changes from by-elections not fully resolved |
| CJP arrests and concessions | **High** | Exact number of still-active FIRs against protesters unknown |
| Ministerial resignation as genuine concession | **High** | — |
| AI surveillance deployment | **Low–Moderate** | Petition filed; no evidentiary ruling; no government transparency report |
| Bihar voter roll deletions | **Low** | Sub judice; no independent audit published |
| EC appointment process structural bias | **High** (structural) | Whether it produces biased operational outcomes: **Low** |
| Judiciary independence | **Moderate–High** | High-visibility cases show independence; lower-visibility cases under-documented |

**What primary data would most improve this assessment:**
1. A published, timestamped register of all FIRs filed against CJP protesters and their current status (withdrawn / active / convicted).
2. An independent audit of Bihar voter rolls before and after SIR, with demographic breakdown — this is the single highest-impact data gap.
3. The Supreme Court's eventual ruling in *Jaya Thakur v. Union of India* on EC appointment constitutionality.
4. Platform transparency reports from X and Meta on Indian government takedown/user-data requests in 2026.
5. A published, public rationale and time-bound mandate for any AI surveillance infrastructure deployed during the protests.

---

## Final Assessment

India in August 2026 sits at **MODERATE** overall risk, with **elevated** sub-indicators in three specific domains: (a) electoral institution independence, (b) online/social media enforcement posture, and (c) the trajectory of coalition arithmetic toward the supermajority threshold.

The clearest finding is a **dual dynamic**: visible, high-profile accountability mechanisms (courts, parliament, public pressure, press) remain operational and produced concrete outcomes during the CJP crisis — this is meaningful. Simultaneously, a pattern of low-visibility enforcement (social media surveillance, platform data requests, AI-tracking allegations) appears to be expanding, and its full scope remains opaque to public scrutiny. The framework's "core operating test" — that significant power use be "externally observable, time-bound where possible, and open to repeated public justification" — is being met selectively: met for high-visibility concessions, partially unmet for enforcement infrastructure.

No evidence currently supports the conclusion that India has crossed into autocratic consolidation. The evidence does support the conclusion that **specific risk vectors are active and should be monitored with primary-source rigour**, particularly electoral institution integrity, the pace of NDA's Rajya Sabha accumulation, and the normalisation of low-visibility digital enforcement.

The Grievance Appellate Committee (GAC), Ministry of Electronics & IT, Government of India, has passed an Order dated 15 July 2026 (Appeal No. 8321/2026) directing YouTube to remove the video titled “Can Hindus Eat Beef? | Kerala Story 2 Exposed” within 24 hours of receiving the Order.

Key points from the GAC Order:

- The video contains deliberate and malicious statements insulting Bhagwan Shri Ram, Bhagwan Shri Krishna, and Sita Devi.

- It falsely claims they consumed meat (including deer meat) and alcohol, using distorted references from scriptures.

- Such content hurts the religious sentiments of crores of Hindus and is against societal harmony.

- YouTube’s arguments on “free speech” were not accepted. Freedom of expression comes with reasonable restrictions under Article 19(2) of the Constitution.

The order was issued after Hon'ble Delhi High Court’s direction on 3rd July 2026 to decide the appeal within 15 days.

Important: This observation and finding by the GAC that the video hurts religious sentiments will also have a strong bearing on the decision of the Ld. Magistrate before whom our petition seeking registration of FIR against Dhruv Rathee is pending for hearing on 10.09.2026.

Faith cannot be mocked under the garb of “content creation.” Justice is being delivered step by step.

UPDATE TO ALL MEMBERS ON LOCUM ENGAGEMENT & CASUALIZATION

The leadership of NARD, ably led by the Strategic P-MUS (Garkuwan Matasan Arewa), is pleased to update members on the outcome of the FMoHSW Committee on  Regulation and Casualization of Doctors.

Following extensive consultations, the Committee has developed a National Policy on the Engagement of Locum, aimed at ensuring fair, transparent and non-exploitative engagement of temporary healthcare personnel.

KEY RECOMMENDATIONS

1. Recruitment & Approval:
   Locum engagement must be based on a clearly identified staffing gap and approved by the appropriate hospital authorities.

2. Contract Duration:
   Initial locum contracts shall not exceed 6 months, with only one additional 6-month renewal permitted. Continuous engagement for 12 months makes the position eligible for permanent appointment.

3. Maximum Work Hours:
   Healthcare personnel shall work a maximum of 48 hours per week, including weekends. Excess hours must be appropriately compensated.

4. Maximum Duty Period:
   No healthcare personnel shall work beyond 24 continuous hours, including call duty.

5. Mandatory Rest:
   
   - Minimum 12 hours between shifts.

   - Mandatory 24-hour post-call rest after weekday and weekend calls.

   - A 1-hour break after 6 hours of continuous work.

6. Call Duty:
   
   - Maximum 2 calls per week.

   - Maximum 1 weekend call per month.

   - Calls must be equitably distributed.

7. Remuneration & Welfare:
Pay rates are standardized in alignment with the government's 
Scheme of Service. Remuneration must be paid monthly without delay, accompanied by monthly 
payslips. 

Locum staff are entitled to all government-approved leaves, public holidays, and occupational insurance coverage.

8. Excess Work Hours:
   Excess hours must be properly documented, monitored and adequately compensated, or appropriately balanced with structured time-off.

9. Protection Against Abuse:
   Locum engagement must not be used as a permanent substitute for substantive recruitment or as a means of exploiting healthcare workers.

10. Integration & Safety: All locum workers must undergo mandatory orientation and integration into their respective clinical or administrative teams. Institutions are required to provide safe 
working environment, adequate call rooms, refreshments during prolonged calls/shifts, and burnout prevention programs.

11. Discipline & Grievance Process: Professional misconduct shall be governed by the regulatory 
council guidelines. Contracts can be terminated by either party with a one-month notice or payment in lieu, and all accrued entitlements must be settled within 14 days of termination. Disputes escalate through institutional mechanisms up to the Federal Ministry of Health and Social Welfare, and the Federal Ministry of Labour and Employment.

12. Monitoring: The Ministry would ensure Institutions do not engage in exploitative staffing practices and violations of this guideline in line with the Nigerian Labour Law.

13. Policy Review and Effective Date:
This policy becomes legally binding on the exact date of approval by the Federal Ministry of 
Health and Social Welfare (FMoH&SW). To ensure its continuous operational relevance, the 
policy mandates a comprehensive evaluation and review within two (2) years of its 
implementation.

The policy is expected to provide a more structured and equitable framework for locum engagement across Nigerian health institutions.

Appreciation to the Hon. Coordinating Minister for Health and Social Welfare, Prof. Mohammad Ali Pate for this approval.

Special appreciation to the Hon. Minister of State for Health and Social Welfare, Dr. Iziak Adekunle Salako for his guidance and dictation to seeing this through.

Appreciations are also in order to our distinguished NARDites in the Committee for a job well done. Thank you Dr. Kwarshak Kevin Yakubu, the VP 2 of NARD. Thank you Dr. Shuaibu Ibrahim, the Secretary General of NARD.

NARD is particularly proud of this accomplishments and proves once again what we can achieve when we come together as a team.

NARD remains committed to protecting the dignity, welfare, rights and professional interests of every Nigerian doctor.

It is our hope that the National Council on Health will also give their stamp of approval on this.

Dr. Abdulmajid Yahya Ibrahim
NARD PSS

@andyburnham Why Do So Many People Vote Against Their Own Best Interests?
From Thatcher's Right to Buy to the global politics of oligarchy
How did Margaret Thatcher persuade millions of British people to applaud the sale of assets they already owned collectively? How did Britain arrive at a country in which water — something as fundamental as the air we breathe — became a collection of private regional monopolies, while successive governments tolerated a system in which sewage is discharged into rivers and seas on an industrial scale? And why, today, across dozens of democracies on every continent, are we allowing some of the world's richest technology companies to make billions from capturing the attention of our children, despite mounting evidence of the damage that excessive social-media use can cause?
These are not isolated national failures. They are local chapters of the same global story: the transformation of citizens into consumers, of public goods into commodities, and of legitimate grievances into resentment against convenient scapegoats. Britain is where this essay begins, because Britain — under Thatcher — is where the modern version of the story was written most explicitly. But the same script has since been performed, with local variations, in Santiago and Buenos Aires, in Moscow and Delhi, in Washington and Brasília, in Budapest and Rome.
The question is how such a transformation became electorally attractive to the very people who would often be most dependent upon the collective institutions being dismantled — and why that same mechanism now operates as a genuinely global political technology, exported, imitated, and refined across borders.
The Thatcher revolution
In the 1970s, while working in a comprehensive school on a council estate where roughly 30 per cent of families were living on benefits and many pupils faced significant learning difficulties, I heard working-class youngsters say they would vote for Margaret Thatcher because she promised to sell them their council houses.
It was easy to understand the appeal. Council housing was not always good housing, and the prospect of owning the home in which your family lived represented something tangible and liberating: security, dignity, a stake in society and perhaps a route into the prosperity enjoyed by people who had always owned property.
The political genius of the Right to Buy was to turn that aspiration into an argument against collective provision. The Housing Act 1980 enabled millions of council tenants to purchase their homes, often at substantial discounts. For many individual families it was an excellent bargain. But the collective consequence was very different. Social housing was being transferred from the public to the private sector, while far too little replacement housing was built.
The Institute for Fiscal Studies has described Right to Buy as the largest source of privatisation revenue to the Treasury and has documented its contribution to the substantial reduction in Britain's social-housing stock. The political transaction was therefore extraordinarily effective: a generation acquired an asset, while the next inherited a country with fewer affordable homes.
The immediate gain was visible; the long-term loss was not.
More importantly, Right to Buy helped change the moral language of British politics — and, in time, the moral language of politics far beyond Britain. The post-war settlement had rested on the idea that some things were too important to be left entirely to the market: healthcare, education, housing, social security and essential infrastructure were collective investments that enlarged the freedom of everyone. Thatcherism gradually replaced that conception with a much harsher proposition: you are responsible for yourself.
Ownership became virtue; dependence became shame. Public provision increasingly appeared as an obstacle to individual aspiration. The citizen was recast as a consumer, the patient as a customer and the tenant as an aspiring property owner. The old language of solidarity, public service and the common good began to sound hopelessly unfashionable.
It was not merely an economic revolution. It was a revolution in what people were encouraged to believe about one another — and it was exported with remarkable speed. Reagan's America ran the same script simultaneously, deregulating and privatising under a nearly identical moral vocabulary. Pinochet's Chile, advised by economists trained in the same free-market tradition, privatised pensions, water rights, and utilities under military rule, with Chile's experience later held up internationally as a model to imitate. When the Soviet Union collapsed, the same doctrine — administered abroad this time, by international institutions rather than domestic politicians — produced Russia's infamous "loans-for-shares" scheme, in which a handful of insiders acquired vast state industries at a fraction of their value and became the oligarchs who define Russian politics to this day. The IMF and World Bank's "structural adjustment" programmes carried a version of the same logic into dozens of countries across Latin America, Africa, and Asia through the 1980s and 1990s, often as a condition of desperately needed loans: sell the state utility, cut the subsidy, open the market, and prosperity will follow.
It rarely did, for the many. It nearly always did, for the few who were positioned to buy.
The great political bait-and-switch
The deeper achievement of Thatcherism — and of every regime that has since copied its playbook — was to persuade people that collective power was an impediment to individual freedom.
If you could buy your house, you had escaped the state. If you could buy shares, you had become a capitalist. If you could make money, you had succeeded. The fact that millions of people could not accumulate comparable wealth, and that public assets sold cheaply could not easily be recreated, was pushed into the background.
The question that should always accompany such policies is the simplest one in politics:
Who benefits?
Who owns the asset after it has been sold? Who receives the rent? Who collects the dividends? Who has the bargaining power? Who bears the risk when the market fails?
Those questions have become even more important as the politics of privatisation has evolved into something larger and more global: the politics of oligarchy.
The new politics of resentment
Donald Trump and Nigel Farage speak in a cruder idiom than Thatcher, but they exploit a related psychological mechanism — and they are far from alone. Narendra Modi in India, Jair Bolsonaro in Brazil, Viktor Orbán in Hungary, Marine Le Pen in France, Giorgia Meloni in Italy, Javier Milei in Argentina: each has built a version of the same politics, tuned to local grievance but running on an identical engine. Their politics feeds on a very real sense that many people have been ignored, humiliated and left behind, while offering an explanation that points almost everywhere except towards concentrated wealth and corporate power.
Your wages have stagnated? Blame immigrants. Your children cannot afford a house? Blame migrants. Your local services are deteriorating? Blame bureaucracy. Your hospital is under pressure? Blame foreigners. Your community is changing? Blame multiculturalism. Your political voice seems weaker? Blame judges, journalists, civil servants, universities or "woke" liberals.
The extraordinary thing about this politics is not that people are angry. They have good reasons to be angry, in London and in Lagos, in Ohio and in Uttar Pradesh. The extraordinary thing is that the anger is so often directed away from those with the greatest power to determine how wealth and opportunity are distributed — and that this misdirection now travels across borders almost as efficiently as capital itself, amplified by social-media platforms and cable-news formats that were, not coincidentally, pioneered and exported from the same handful of countries.
The migrant did not privatise your water. The refugee did not abolish your council house. The teacher did not create the housing shortage. The nurse did not weaken your trade union. The civil servant did not turn housing into an investment vehicle. The person on benefits did not accumulate billions.
The politics of resentment succeeds by taking genuine suffering and supplying a false explanation for it — and it succeeds in remarkably similar ways whether the suffering is a British tenant priced out of the town they grew up in, an American factory worker whose plant relocated abroad, or a Brazilian farmer squeezed by global commodity prices.
The promise of power to the powerless
Authoritarian populism begins with a seductive proposition, wherever it appears: you are powerless only because somebody has stolen your power. Identify the traitors, the migrants, the liberals, the judges, the feminists, the environmentalists, the welfare claimants, the journalists or whatever other convenient enemy the political moment requires, and everything can be restored.
The leader then performs a remarkable psychological trick. His power becomes the voter's power. His contempt becomes their revenge. His refusal to accept restraints becomes their freedom. His attacks on democratic institutions become evidence of his courage. His ignorance becomes authenticity and his lies become "telling it like it is".
This is why the rhetoric of "ordinary people" — or "the real Americans", or "the real Hungarians", or "Bharat" as against a supposedly Westernised elite — is so important everywhere it appears. It rarely means everyone who is ordinary. It means a carefully constructed image of the right sort of ordinary person: respectable, patriotic, hard-working, native, suspicious of outsiders and resentful of people supposedly receiving favours denied to them.
Once that imaginary population has been defined as "the people", almost anyone can be declared their enemy.
Identity instead of security
The bargain offered by the global Hard Right is therefore remarkably stark, and remarkably consistent from country to country: surrender material security and collective power in exchange for symbolic superiority.
You may have less affordable housing, weaker trade unions, poorer public services, insecure employment, diminished legal protections and a less reliable social safety net. But you will be told that you are nevertheless more free because someone else — the migrant, the welfare claimant, the "woke" academic, the environmentalist, the metropolitan liberal — has been put in his or her place.
It is a paper crown, minted in slightly different designs for each national market, but stamped from the same die.
And human beings are not economic calculators. They vote with memory, identity, fear, pride, resentment and hope. A person who feels humiliated can sometimes prefer the emotional satisfaction of seeing somebody else humiliated to the material benefits of a policy that does not flatter his identity.
That is why the politics of resentment can survive policies that make the lives of many of its supporters harder — in Britain, in America, in India, in Hungary, in Brazil.
From democracy to oligarchy
The ultimate danger is that this politics does not produce greater popular power anywhere it takes hold. It produces oligarchy: a global class whose wealth is so concentrated, and so mobile across borders, that it can purchase political influence, media influence, technological power and privileged access to the machinery of government in country after country.
Democracy can survive formally while becoming increasingly hollow. There can still be elections, political parties and parliamentary debates, while a tiny minority — increasingly the same tiny minority, moving capital fluidly between London, New York, Dubai, and offshore jurisdictions that exist precisely to make wealth hard to trace — possesses a vastly disproportionate capacity to determine what citizens see, what politicians hear and which policies are considered politically possible.
The danger is not simply that billionaires become extraordinarily rich in any one country. It is that wealth becomes power, power becomes influence, influence shapes policy, and policy allows wealth to become still more concentrated — and that this cycle now operates at a planetary scale, largely beyond the reach of any single national electorate to correct. A British voter can vote out a British government. No electorate, anywhere, can currently vote out the architecture of tax havens, shell companies, and cross-border capital flows that lets the same fortunes migrate just ahead of whatever regulation any one country manages to pass.
That is a self-reinforcing political machine, and it is a global one.
Look at the water
Britain's privatised water industry offers an almost perfect case study — and it is far from unique.
England and Wales privatised their water companies in 1989, creating regional private monopolies in which consumers have little meaningful choice over their supplier. The promise was that private capital and commercial discipline would deliver greater efficiency and investment.
Yet the environmental record is increasingly difficult to defend. In England alone, official figures for 2024 recorded 450,398 monitored sewage-spill events, lasting more than 3.6 million hours. There were 2,801 pollution incidents caused by water and sewerage assets, including 75 serious incidents — the highest number of serious incidents since 2013.
This is what happens when a public necessity is treated principally as a commercial asset. The customer cannot simply shop elsewhere. The river cannot complain. The sewage system cannot threaten to take its business to a competitor.
Britain is not alone in learning this lesson the hard way. Bolivia's attempt to privatise the water supply of Cochabamba in 2000, under World Bank pressure, led to price rises so severe that ordinary citizens could no longer afford water for cooking or bathing — and to an uprising so fierce that the government was forced to reverse the privatisation within months. Jakarta privatised its water system in 1998 and spent the next two decades failing to deliver clean water to large parts of the city before a court finally ordered the system back into public hands. City after city that once privatised water — Paris, Berlin, Buenos Aires, Atlanta — has since taken it back into public ownership, in a global pattern now recognised by researchers as "remunicipalisation."
The private monopoly therefore possesses something very close to the perfect commercial position, in Britain or Bolivia alike: captive customers and a public that ultimately cannot allow the essential infrastructure to collapse.
The political question is not whether every water executive, in any country, is a villain. It is much simpler:
Why should an essential natural monopoly be organised primarily around private financial interests at all?
Now Silicon Valley wants our children's attention — everywhere
The same philosophy is now moving into a new, borderless territory: the human mind, of children on every continent simultaneously.
The great technology platforms have discovered that attention itself can be monetised, and monetised identically whether the child in question lives in Manchester, Manila, or Minneapolis. Children are no longer simply children in this business model; they are users, data points and sources of advertising revenue. The commercial incentive is to maximise engagement, and therefore to develop systems capable of learning precisely what keeps an individual user returning — a system indifferent to the nationality of the child it is designed to hold.
The American Surgeon General has warned that social media can pose a meaningful risk to young people and that adolescents who spend more than three hours a day on social media face approximately twice the risk of experiencing mental-health problems. This is not an American finding about American children. It is a description of an engagement architecture built once and deployed globally, at essentially zero marginal cost per additional country.
Yet the commercial machine continues to depend upon capturing attention, everywhere it can be captured.
We have seen this pattern before, and it too was global. Tobacco companies did not voluntarily abandon a profitable product because early evidence suggested harm — and having lost that argument in wealthy countries with strong regulators, they simply redirected their marketing towards countries with weaker ones, where smoking rates are now rising fastest. Fossil-fuel companies did not enthusiastically reorganise their businesses around the climate consequences of burning their products, and the costs of that delay are being paid disproportionately by countries that contributed least to the emissions. Industries organised around profit naturally resist regulation that threatens the business model, and naturally seek out whichever jurisdiction regulates them least.
The question is therefore not whether technology is "good" or "bad", in Britain or anywhere else. It is whether democratic governments — acting together, since no single government can discipline a company that can simply route around it — are prepared to regulate immensely powerful, genuinely global corporations when their commercial incentives conflict with the interests of children.
Who are the real elites?
This exposes one of the great contradictions of modern populism, and it holds in almost identical form on every continent where the populist playbook has been run.
The Hard Right constantly rails against "the elites". Yet its political movements require enormous resources: advertising, professional campaigning, data, media exposure and wealthy donors — resources that increasingly cross borders as freely as everything else in this story. The rhetoric says: I am fighting the establishment. The obvious question is: which establishment?
The populist politician may denounce the metropolitan elite while being surrounded by people who possess vastly more wealth and influence than the voters he claims to represent — whether that is a British tabloid proprietor, an American tech billionaire, an Indian industrialist, or a Hungarian oligarch who happens to be the prime minister's childhood friend. The billionaire becomes a heroic rebel; the public-sector worker becomes part of the problem.
It is an extraordinary inversion, and it repeats itself, almost word for word, from parliament to parliament.
The politics that most loudly denounces elites can become the politics that protects them.
The fascist temptation
It would be both inaccurate and politically foolish to describe every Trump, Farage, Modi, Bolsonaro, or Le Pen voter as a fascist. Many are simply angry people who have concluded, often for understandable reasons, that the political system no longer works for them, wherever in the world they happen to live.
But the techniques of authoritarian populism have a disturbing historical pedigree, and they travel with remarkably little translation required: invent an idealised "real people"; identify internal enemies; blame minorities for national decline; attack independent institutions; ridicule experts; weaken the press; glorify strength; promise national restoration; and present the leader as the embodiment of popular will.
The lesson of the 1930s is not that every contemporary populist, in any country, is Hitler. It is that democracies can be weakened incrementally, through the destruction of trust in the institutions that restrain power — and that this weakening now happens on a strikingly similar timetable in country after country, sometimes with direct coordination and mutual admiration between leaders who present themselves as national, even nationalist, but who study and borrow one another's methods with real internationalist enthusiasm.
First the judge becomes the enemy. Then the journalist. Then the civil servant. Then the teacher. Then the scientist. Then the university.
Eventually almost anybody who questions the Leader can be portrayed as an enemy of the people — in Washington or in Brasília, in Budapest or in New Delhi.
Democracy does not necessarily die with a bang, anywhere. It can be hollowed out while the elections continue.
The answer is not to insult the voters
The answer, therefore, is not to sneer at people who vote for populists, in Britain or anywhere else. That simply reinforces the very resentment on which the populists feed.
People are angry because real things have happened, on every continent. Housing really is unaffordable, from London to Los Angeles to Auckland. Public services really have been degraded. Wages really have stagnated for millions. Wealth really has become grotesquely concentrated — the world's richest handful of individuals now hold more wealth than billions of people combined. Communities really have declined. Political institutions really have become remote from many people's lives.
The task of democratic politics, everywhere, is to say: your anger is justified. But you have been lied to about its cause.
Your neighbour did not steal your future. The refugee did not privatise your water. The person receiving benefits did not buy the newspapers. The teacher did not turn your home into an investment asset. The nurse did not weaken your bargaining power.
Look upwards. Look at who owns things. Look at who receives the rent and dividends. Look at who funds the political campaigns. Look at who owns the media. Look at who controls the platforms. Look at who writes the rules — and notice how often it is the same small set of names and funds, operating under different flags in different countries.
Follow the money. It rarely stops at any border.
Freedom is not the absence of society
The great political fraud of our time — global in its reach, local in its costumes — is to define freedom as the absence of collective obligation.
Real freedom is rather different, in Bristol or in Buenos Aires. A child is freer when she has a good school; a sick person is freer when healthcare is available without financial terror; a worker is freer when she can negotiate with her employer on something approaching equal terms; a family is freer when it can afford a decent home; and a citizen is freer when the water coming from the tap is safe and the river flowing past the town is not being used as a sewer.
These things are not handouts from a benevolent state. They are the infrastructure of freedom, and no country has yet found a way to manufacture that infrastructure through private markets alone.
Without them, freedom becomes something that can increasingly be purchased rather than possessed — available, in full, only to the people who no longer need politics to protect it.
And that brings us back to the original question.
Why do people, in country after country, sometimes vote against their own economic interests?
Because politics is not merely about economics. It is about meaning, dignity, belonging and power. If democratic politics cannot give people a convincing account of their suffering, the demagogue will provide one — and increasingly, the same demagogic playbook, adapted overnight for a new market. If it cannot offer them hope, resentment will fill the vacuum. If it cannot persuade them that solidarity is a source of strength, somebody else will persuade them that cruelty is.
The choice before us is therefore much larger than Thatcherism, or Trump, or Farage, or any single national election.
It is between two fundamentally different conceptions of freedom, being decided simultaneously in dozens of countries, often by people who have never met but who are, in the ways that matter, fighting the same fight.
One says: you are on your own; buy whatever security you can afford, and blame somebody poorer than yourself for the rest.
The other says: we are citizens of the same society — and, increasingly, of the same interconnected world — and some things are too important to be left to whoever happens to have the most money.
The first road leads towards oligarchy, wherever it is walked.
The second leads back towards democracy.
And the central political task of this generation, in London and Lagos, in Delhi and Detroit, is to make the second road more attractive than the first — everywhere, before the first road closes behind us for good.

🚨 BIG: Government of India has unveiled one of the most comprehensive legal frameworks to combat AI-generated deepfakes, synthetic media, misinformation and unlawful online content.

The framework brings together the IT Act, 2000, Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita (BNS), 2023, IT Rules, 2021, the 2026 IT Rules amendments, and the IndiaAI Governance Guidelines to strengthen digital safety and platform accountability.

Key highlights:

🔹 Mandatory AI Labelling: Platforms must clearly label AI-generated or synthetic content with traceable metadata so users can identify manipulated content and prevent deception.

🔹 Fastest Takedown Timelines Yet: Removal of unlawful content after a valid government or court notice has been reduced from 36 hours to just 3 hours. Grievance redressal timelines have also been tightened—from 72 hours to 36 hours, and 24 hours to 2 hours for sensitive content such as nudity, impersonation and similar categories.

🔹 IT Act, 2000: Covers penalties for computer-related offences, identity theft (Sec. 66C), online impersonation (66D), privacy violations (66E), publishing obscene or sexually explicit content (Secs. 67 & 67A), empowers blocking of unlawful content under Sec. 69A, removal directions under Sec. 79, and enables police investigation under Secs. 78 & 80.

🔹 Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita, 2023: Covers cheating by personation (Sec. 319), forgery through false electronic records (Sec. 336), spreading false reports or misinformation causing public mischief (Sec. 353), and organised cybercrime involving deepfake content (Sec. 111).

🔹 Strict Platform Obligations: Intermediaries must not host or share content that infringes rights, invades privacy, promotes hate or violence, harms children, violates intellectual property, misleads users about message origin, knowingly spreads false information, impersonates individuals (including using AI), threatens India's sovereignty, security or public order, or violates any applicable law.

🔹 Greater Accountability for Social Media Platforms: Significant Social Media Intermediaries (SSMIs) must assist law enforcement in tracing originators of serious content, deploy automated tools to detect unlawful content, publish compliance reports, appoint grievance and compliance officers, maintain India-based compliance infrastructure, and provide user verification, appeals and fair hearing mechanisms.

🔹 Zero Tolerance for Harmful AI: Platforms are now explicitly required to prevent AI-generated child sexual abuse material, non-consensual intimate imagery, deepfakes, AI impersonation, harmful synthetic media and other unlawful AI-generated content using reasonable technical measures and automated detection systems.

🔹 Legal Consequences: Failure to comply with the IT Rules can result in intermediaries losing their Section 79 safe-harbour protection, exposing them to prosecution and legal action under applicable laws.

🔹 Robust Enforcement Ecosystem: The framework will be enforced through Grievance Appellate Committees (GACs), the Indian Cyber Crime Coordination Centre (I4C), the SAHYOG Portal, the National Cyber Crime Reporting Portal, and law enforcement agencies. Citizens can report cybercrime and deepfakes through the National Cyber Crime Reporting Portal, with Helpline 1930 available for cyber fraud complaints.

🔹 Responsible AI Development: Under the IndiaAI Mission, the government is funding indigenous AI safety projects, including Saakshya (IIT Jodhpur & IIT Madras), AI Vishleshak, and IIT Kharagpur's Real-Time Voice Deepfake Detection System, alongside the India AI Governance Guidelines to promote safe, trusted and responsible AI deployment.

The message is clear: AI innovation is welcome, but deepfakes, impersonation, misinformation, child exploitation, and unlawful synthetic content will face significantly stricter regulation, faster takedowns, and stronger legal consequences than ever before.

When the summer of 2022 rolled in, I was able to make up for lost time on the road until 2023 when I was ready to head to St. Petersburg, Florida and take some well-earned time to write. It was in early 2024 after sending him my cover version of his song “Traveling Alone” that Jason Isbell and I first talked about working together, and incredibly he offered to produce these songs, enlisting Gena Johnson as co-producer. 

Pinch me.

Fast forward to September 2024 - Jason, Gena and I started making this album at Sound Emporium in Nashville. Jason enlisted members of the 400 Unit to be our rhythm section. We recorded the songs that eventually became the 10 tracks on “Billionaire”. I am so indebted and thankful to Jason and Gena for their dedication, their time, their care and their talents - in championing me and my work, and to all the musicians who appear on this album coming out August 22nd.

Songs that tell the story of looking through the rear view mirror on my way to something new, watching a version of myself and my life behind me get smaller on the horizon as I go. Fact Check: JF-17 Block III Production and Exports

Indian propaganda accounts are falsely claiming that Pakistan has slowed down production of the JF-17 Block III fighter jet. The claim is misleading and not backed by evidence.

Production Status
By mid-2025, Pakistan has already produced around 23 Block III jets, with the Kamra facility on track to complete the full 30-unit order. This shows production is proceeding as planned, not “slowed down” as alleged.

Export Success
Far from lacking orders, Pakistan has secured a landmark deal with Azerbaijan for 40 JF-17 Block III jets. This is one of Pakistan’s biggest defense export agreements, proving both the demand and credibility of the aircraft on the global stage.

Cost Reality
The figure of $55 million per jet is misleading. That price includes weapons, training, spare parts, and support packages. The base cost of the jet itself remains around $25 million, making it one of the most cost-effective 4.5 generation fighters available.

The narrative pushed by Indian disinformation accounts is baseless. The JF-17 Block III program remains on schedule, expanding Pakistan’s air power and earning major international contracts. A. “Collapse of sincerity” vs “Working constitutional speech-market” — juxtaposed refutation

Claim (Mehta): algorithms monetise performance; sincerity is dead.

Counter (law-anchored): India’s system builds, protects, and disciplines truthful communication.

Free speech spine intact: Art.19(1)(a); limits only under Art.19(2)—sovereignty, integrity (via 16th Amend., 1963), public order, decency, contempt, defamation, incitement.

Shreya Singhal (2015): struck 66A IT Act; mandated narrow tests (“incitement”, “tendency to create”). Sincerity space preserved.

Right to know fuels deliberation: PUCL v. Union (2003) & ADR (2002)—candidate disclosures as Art.19(1)(a); RTI Act 2005 operationalises truth access, not performance.

State coercion checked: Anuradha Bhasin (2020)—internet restrictions must be proportional, reasoned, reviewable. Kaushal Kishor (2023)—remedies exist for ministerial speech harm; no blanket gag on political speech.

Harmful speech contained, not chilled: Subramanian Swamy (2016) upheld criminal defamation to protect Art.21 reputation; Amish Devgan (2020) clarified hate-speech thresholds—ethics by law, not by vibe.

Platform due-diligence (not censorship): IT (Intermediary Guidelines & Digital Media Ethics Code) Rules, 2021—grievance officers, 36-hr takedown on court/LEA orders, traceability for heinous crimes; 69A IT Act blocking only via speaking orders + review (per Shreya Singhal).

Election truth-checks: Model Code of Conduct, cVIGIL, paid-news rules; ECI + SVEEP strengthen voter information.

Civic transparency expanding: Open Government Data, Proactive RTI (s.4), Social Audit (MNREGA/SSA rules)—institutionalise fact visibility.

Bottom line: The architecture prizes sincerity by rights (19(1)(a)), guardrails (19(2)), remedies (courts/RTI/ECI). The market is noisy; the constitution makes it corrigible.
