IFF's statement on the AI Impact Summit 2026.

The Internet Freedom Foundation (IFF) welcomes the India AI Impact Summit 2026 (February 16-20) as an important platform for global dialogue on, "Artificial Intelligence". We believe the Summit's agenda and framing fundamentally misalign with the lived reality of AI deployment in India, an environment marked by rising digital authoritarianism and the systematic erosion of constitutional protections that are causing demonstrable harm to vulnerable populations. Its official framing centers on “People, Planet and Progress”, with Prime Minister Narendra Modi inaugurating and world leaders like France’s President Emmanuel Macron and top tech CEOs (Google’s Sundar Pichai, OpenAI’s Sam Altman, etc.) expected to attend. The Summit's optimistic narrative about AI for development obscures the reality of how its deployment is impacting people in their everyday lives.

The current environment is one of a sharp contraction in civic space, where recent governance proposals on technology have facilitated the expansion of state power that run contrary to the state commitments on fundamental rights and social justice. Today, there exists few organisations in India that work on digital rights and those which are surviving are severely under resourced, suffer from burdensome compliances, growing legal risks and deliberate exclusion from policy making processes. The decline of civil society work is matching the growth of private and public sector capacity to lobby the policy making processes. So, even before a question is prompted, how should Indian civil society engage with the India AI Impact Summit, a predicate and grounded inquiry is, how many independent, Indian civil society groups exist in India that have capacity and can be critical of state policies and practices around AI?

In the recent past, far from fostering accountability, India’s digitisation drive is often used to sidestep constitutional safeguards of transparency, harming communities and individuals. For instance, recent legal changes have weakened the Right to Information (RTI) framework, curtailing citizens’ ability to question power. The Digital Personal Data Protection (DPDP) Act, 2023 introduced an amendment (Section 8(1)(j) to the RTI Act) that blocks access to any information labeled “personal information”, allowing officials to deny critical information. Likewise, digitisation of welfare governance has been weaponized to bypass accountability, with digitisation often becoming a gatekeeper and working to the detriment of the poor. A stark development came in December, 2025 when Parliament hastily passed the Viksit Bharat - Guarantee for Rozgar and Ajeevika Mission (Gramin) Act, 2025 (VB-GRAM G), repealing the landmark MGNREGA jobs guarantee program. VB-GRAM G converted a demand driven legal right to work into a discretionary, bureaucratically controlled scheme, undermining decades of workers’ rights. There are references to "AI" within the text of the objects and reasons that are a part of this law.

Beyond this, India's policies on AI also demonstrate a wider embrace of de-regulation narratives to ensure, "innovation". For instance, the Union Budget 2026 unveiled a 20-year tax holiday (until 2047) for foreign firms using Indian data centers, aiming to lure global AI infrastructure. Yet, this policy was formulated with scant regard for its impact on local communities and natural resources. Other recent measures also deserve comment:

Sanchar Saathi : In late 2025, the government ordered smartphone manufacturers to pre-install a government cybersecurity application called Sanchar Saathi on all devices. The app was ostensibly meant to secure citizens’ phones, but the mandatory installation sparked outrage over privacy and surveillance concerns, drawing parallels to spyware abuse.
The ‘Sahyog’ Censorship Portal: In 2024, the Union Home Ministry quietly launched the Sahyog Portal to expedite content-blocking orders on social media and websites. Under this system, law enforcement agencies can flag “unlawful” online content and directly trigger its takedown by internet platforms, all through a centralized interface.
Expansion of NATGRID: Perhaps the most far-reaching is the quiet expansion of NATGRID, India’s National Intelligence Grid. Long conceived as an integrated database for counter-terror investigations, NATGRID has recently morphed into a broad surveillance net. Following a high-level police conference in late November 2025, states were directed to “scale up” NATGRID usage beyond central agencies, even giving police officers at the Superintendent rank access to its vast datasets.
These developments match the increased use of AI technologies in domains of policing and welfare without a clear legal basis and real safeguards.

IFF acknowledges that the India AI Impact Summit 2026 offers a platform for dialogue and a chance for civil society voices to gain visibility on an international stage. We recognize the value in having digital rights perspectives included in global AI governance conversations, indeed, the Summit’s presence in India is an opportunity to spotlight our constitutional concerns before a world audience. We support our peer organizations and allies who choose to engage with the Summit, and we will remain in constructive collaboration with them. However, IFF has decided not to allocate significant organizational resources to direct participation in the Summit’s events. This is not a boycott of the forum, but a practical choice of focus. As a small team of only 7 full-time staff based in New Delhi, we must prioritize the most pressing advocacy initiatives that align closely with our mission and charter.

This includes ongoing efforts such as legal challenges to unconstitutional regulations, campaigning and community engagement for strengthening free expression, privacy and transparency frameworks. These are battles immediately affecting citizens’ rights and requiring our sustained attention. IFF will engage with the Summit in a mindful, critical manner. We will track the proceedings and outcomes closely, offering our analyses and critiques rooted in constitutional values. If and where we do participate (for example, in side events or discussions), we will do so with a critical gaze, centering the lived experiences of Indians and the paramountcy of our fundamental rights. Our support is firmly with the broader civil society coalition pushing for AI governance that is accountable and just.

When Electoral Revision Becomes a Test of Democracy

A Newslaundry investigation has uncovered a deeply troubling pattern in Uttarakhand’s ongoing Special Intensive Revision (SIR) of electoral rolls.

Five of the highest-volume objectors across Uttarakhand’s 70 Assembly constituencies are BJP-linked workers. Together, they filed about 6,500 objections, and Newslaundry found that every voter targeted by these five men was Muslim. In some constituencies, a single individual accounted for 90–99% of all deletion requests. 

The numbers are striking.

Kichha: 4,857 objections; 4,855 filed by one BJP-linked booth-level agent.

Gadarpur: 1,370 objections; 670 from one BJP-linked objector, all against Muslim voters.

Khatima: 394 objections; 392 from one BJP-linked worker.

Nanakmatta: 391 Form-7 applications; 353 from one BJP-linked BLA.

Rudrapur: 2,818 deletion requests, with several large lists submitted by BJP-linked individuals. 

Now, let's be absolutely clear:

An objection is not a deletion.

The BJP says these are legitimate attempts to identify duplicate or shifted voters, particularly because several Uttarakhand constituencies border Uttar Pradesh. Electoral officers have also said that affected voters will receive notices, verification will take place and no deletion should occur without due process. 

That defence must be taken seriously.

But it does not answer the central democratic question:

Why are extraordinarily large numbers of objections being concentrated in the hands of a few politically affiliated individuals—and why do the targeted names show such a striking religious pattern?

That question demands transparent investigation.

There is another important issue.

The Election Commission's 2023 electoral-roll manual had safeguards around bulk applications: a party BLA was permitted to submit no more than 10 applications a day, with additional verification requirements when large numbers were submitted. Newslaundry reports that these restrictions were subsequently modified, including a January 2026 communication for West Bengal that removed the numerical ceiling while requiring additional review above five applications from one objector. 

But one Uttarakhand ERO, when asked to justify the unlimited-volume approach, reportedly pointed to the West Bengal communication—without providing a specific Uttarakhand notification establishing the same rule. 

That deserves clarification from the Election Commission itself.

Because the right to vote is not merely another government benefit.

It is the foundation through which citizens choose their government.

If a genuine duplicate voter is removed, that protects the integrity of elections.

But if a genuine citizen is wrongly removed, the damage is fundamentally different: the citizen may lose the ability to participate in the election that determines who governs them.

And when the people being challenged overwhelmingly belong to one religious community, the burden of proof and scrutiny must be exceptionally rigorous.

The Election Commission's own Form-7 framework places the onus of substantiating the reason for an objection on the applicant. 

So the principle should be simple:

The citizen should not have to prove their loyalty to democracy.
The person seeking their deletion should have to prove the case.

No genuine voter should lose their franchise because somebody submitted a spreadsheet.

No community should have to collectively defend its citizenship because its names appear on somebody's political list.

And no political party—whether BJP, Congress or anyone else—should be allowed to treat the electoral roll as a battlefield for demographic engineering.

The Election Commission must therefore publish transparent, constituency-wise data on:

1. Who filed the objections;

2. How many objections each person filed;

3. The reasons cited;

Cont'd..
Source: [Newslaundry — “Inside the bulk objections targeting Muslims in Uttarakhand’s SIR”](https://t.co/icpZAu1LOQ)

4. The number of objections accepted or rejected;

5. The number of voters actually removed;

6. The demographic pattern of the challenged voters;

7. The verification and hearing process followed in every case.

Because SIR should clean electoral rolls—not clean them of inconvenient voters.

The ultimate test is not how many names are deleted.

It is how many eligible citizens remain protected in the electoral roll.

An election is free and fair only when every eligible citizen has an equal opportunity to cast a vote.

The voter list is not the property of the ruling party.
It belongs to the citizen.

And protecting that list is one of the Election Commission's most sacred democratic responsibilities.

The Silent Emergency: Eleven Years Under the Shadow of Control

India, the land of a billion vibrant voices, is grappling with a chilling silence. For eleven years under the PM, we've witnessed an

"Undeclared Emergency@11"

—no declared curfews, no tanks, but a steady erosion of our democratic freedoms. This is the story of a Nation fighting for its soul, where the cost of speaking out grows heavier daily.

The Press in Chains
Our Fourth Estate, once a beacon of truth, now falters under relentless pressure. V-Dem and Freedom House 2025 reports label India an “electoral autocracy,” ranked “partly free.” The Press Freedom Index places us at 159/176, near Somalia’s shadow. Honest journalists face arrests, raids, and intimidation for daring to question. Laws like UAPA and sedition are weaponized, branding critics “terrorists” without trial. Media houses face raids, their voices stifled. Modi’s 11-year tenure without a single press conference speaks volumes—hate speech thrives, but truth is jailed.

Homes Turned to Rubble
Bulldozers roar across India, not for progress but as tools of vengeance. Homes, often of minorities or dissenters, are demolished in displays of state power. Families stand amid rubble, targeted for their identity or beliefs. Ministers spewing hate are rewarded, while citizens live in fear. This isn’t the India we fought for.

The Digital Gag
In the age of X, FB, Insta, and YouTube, where voices once soared, dissent is now caged. Content creators and tweeters face arrests for “misinformation” or “inciting unrest.” Over 20,000 independent voices have been silenced, their crime often a post challenging the regime. This is a democracy where keyboards are as dangerous as megaphones.

Opposition Under Siege
The Enforcement Directorate (ED) has become a weapon to intimidate opposition leaders, with raids targeting those who refuse to bow to the BJP. Homes and offices of opposition figures are stormed, cases piled up to coerce them into joining the ruling party or face relentless harassment. This blatant misuse of agencies undermines democracy, turning dissent into a dangerous act.

Puppet Election Commission
The Election Commission, once a pillar of democratic integrity, now dances to the tune of the BJP. The removal of the Chief Justice of India from the selection committee for appointing Election Commissioners has raised alarms about its independence. This move, critics argue, ensures a pliable EC, ready to tilt the electoral scales. Free and fair elections, the heartbeat of democracy, now pulse under the shadow of control.

The Leader’s Shadow
Modi’s image dominates—billboards, screens, even vaccine certificates and rail tickets. Supporters call it leadership; we see a cult stifling dissent. Parliament weakened, constitutional bodies eroded, divisive figures glorified—this is a five-fold assault on our democracy. BJP invokes 1975’s Emergency to deflect, but today’s control needs no formal name. It’s a slow, silent strangulation of our freedoms.

Nation’s Resolve
Fifty years ago, India resisted the 1975 Emergency. Today, the shackles are subtler but real. Jailed journalists, bulldozed homes, silenced voices, ED raids on opposition leaders, and a compromised Election Commission tell of a democracy under siege. As Modi marks “Samvidhan Hatya Diwas,” we say the real threat to our Constitution is now—unnamed, insidious, but ever-present.

India stands at a crossroads. Will we reclaim our chorus of voices or let silence prevail? The fight for our democracy lies in the courage of those who speak, write, and dream of a free tomorrow.

text:
In 2024 December, Indian security forces recovered a Starlink antenna/router alongside weapons from militants in northeast India.

The markings on the device indicated that they were brought in from Myanmar across the border.

Reports also indicated that a lot of these devices had been smuggled across the border. Internet signals were spilling over from Myanmar, and bad actors used them to bypass prolonged internet shutdowns during times of unrest.

Allowing internet infrastructure to be operated from outside the country makes it difficult for the government to effectively implement law-and-order measures in critical areas.

This has recently happened in many parts of the world, including Iran, according to news reports. This is what worries the Indian security agencies.

Satellite internet is not limited by boundaries. Agreed that the coverage can still be restricted or managed. Still, that control sits with a company operating from a foreign land.

On top of that, 100% foreign ownership is also spooking the authorities.

The technology is definitely useful and would help reduce the internet coverage gap FAST. But that would also open the door to misuse in places that India is most worried about, i.e., conflict zones, protests, and contested borders.

This is one of the sharpest test cases for satellite internet penetration in India, and it will be interesting to see how it plays out.

Statement : Shutting down Telegram is a band aid solution and is a disproportionate answer to exam fraud

The Internet Freedom Foundation objects to the directions announced today in the National Testing Agency's press release on action against the Telegram platform. On the NTA's recommendation, the Ministry of Electronics and Information Technology has, under Section 69A of the Information Technology Act, 2000, restricted access to the whole of Telegram in India until 22 June 2026, and has separately ordered the platform to switch off message-editing for every Indian user until 30 June 2026. This is a blunt, nationwide measure aimed at the conduct of rampant fraud rackets, and on the Government's own admission is constitutionally incompatible.

At the outset it is important to note that Section 69A and the Blocking Rules of 2009 framed under it allow the Government to block access to specific “information” on a computer resource. They do not extend to switching off an entire intermediary, still less to ordering a company to redesign its product by removing a feature for a whole country. In Shreya Singhal v Union of India, the Supreme Court upheld Section 69A because it is narrow and hedged with procedural safeguards. Reading it to authorise shutting down a platform that lakhs use is an overbroad restriction by the NTAs own admission. For the message-editing direction the release identifies no source of power at all. If one exists, the order must say so.

The release argues against itself

A restriction on access has to be the least intrusive measure that achieves its aim as per the constitutional test of proportionality laid down in Justice K.S. Puttaswamy v. Union of India (2017) and applied in Anuradha Bhasin v. Union of India (2020). The NTA's own narration shows the block fails its nodal agency, the release says, “has secured the prompt take-down of a substantial number of Telegram channels, groups and bots”, and this targeted work “is the reason the harm caused by these rackets has been contained to the extent it has”. If channel level takedown contained the harm, the case for a blanket block collapses and hence the Government has reached for a heavier tool while conceding that a lighter one was working. The collateral cost sits on the record too as noted in the press release. The block, the NTA accepts, “affects lakhs of citizens who use the Telegram platform for legitimate personal, educational, professional and informational purposes”. The release also says there is "no such paper available outside the secured examination chain" and that “the security of the examination is unaffected by the action taken”. If the exam is secure and no leak exists, what is being suppressed is rumour, and rumour cannot justify closing a platform when specific blocking and criminal prosecution remain available.

Students use of Telegram

The block of telegram is reactive and ineffective and will punish ordinary users instead of addressing the systemic source of exam leaks. This blocking comes in the final days of NEET preparation, when thousands of students depend on Telegram for study groups, doubt-clearing, and shared resources. Also, it is important to consider that the source of exam papers leak will occur from inside the system, among insiders and across the printing and logistics chain, with the platform being the most downstream channel for distribution. Hence, switching off Telegram, is merely a deflection from the repeated failures that will continue while media attention is directed towards this Telegram ban.

Lack of transparency

At present only a press release from the NTA has been provided, which recommended the block but the reasoned order of MeitY, the authority that issued it, has not been released. The Anuradha Bhasin decision requires that orders restricting access be published so they can be tested in court. Here the order, and the reasoning of the committee behind it, stay out of view, and we do not know whether Telegram was heard at all. An announcement of a block is no substitute for an order the affected party can challenge.
Blunt to enforce and very easy to evade
Usually, app-level blocks run through IS-level DNS and IP filtering. They are over inclusive, sweeping in lawful use, yet simple to evade as a determined exam leak racket moves to a VPN or a mirror within minutes while ordinary users lose the service for a week.

We ask the Government to:

1) Publish the MeitY Section 69A order and the NTA recommendation behind it, with reasons;
2) State the legal basis for the message editing direction, or withdraw it;
3) Confirm whether Telegram was given a hearing under the Blocking Rules, and place the committee's record before any court that hears a challenge; and
4) Lift the platform-wide restriction and rely on the targeted takedowns the NTA itself credits with containing the harm.

We emphasise that the NEET (UG) 2026 re-examination is worth protecting and it concerns the future of lakhs of aspirants. It requires securing the entire process of examination rather than reaching for purported band aid solutions that instead cause more harm. The State cannot switch off a service used by lakhs to answer the wrongdoing of a few, and cannot do it through an order no one affected is allowed to read. On its own facts, the Government has done both.

New Delhi, 16 June 2026.

Public statement regarding @glen_mcgregor (CityNews / Parliament Hill)
I am posting this for the record.
Glen McGregor publicly posted details about former Liberal MP Shaun Chen’s car accident, including claims of a serious head injury and supporting documentation. I questioned specific points that did not add up — the timeline, the next-day vote in the House, the completeness and authenticity of the report that was shared, and related inconsistencies — using facts and publicly available information.
He chose to reply to me under my account (@Cdhd123 / Not So Nice Canadian). That opened a direct exchange. I continued to respond with fact-based pushback. I did not insult, threaten, or harass him. I said nothing that violated any platform rules.
After engaging with me, he blocked me.
Because he is based in Ottawa covering Parliament Hill, and because Canadian taxpayers indirectly support the media ecosystem that employs journalists in that role, I find it unacceptable that a reporter can post claims, engage with a critic who raises legitimate questions, and then shut that critic out so they can no longer see or respond to further statements.
I will be contacting the relevant ombudsman / oversight body to formally complain about this conduct. Blocking a citizen who asked questions after the journalist himself chose to engage does not serve transparency or accountability.
I have every right to comment on a public post. He had every right to reply or not reply. Once he chose to engage, unilaterally removing my ability to follow the conversation is, in my view, unfair and inconsistent with the standards expected of someone in his position.
This is the public record of what occurred.
— Not So Nice Canadian (@Cdhd123)
@glen_mcgregor @CBC @CTV @CarymaRules @PierrePoilievre @liberal_party @CBCOmbud

Dear @nelsonchamisa,

In responding to this post, I am once again doing my work as a journalist. You have publicly accused me of lying because I said that CCC had neither a proper constitution nor a clearly defined leadership structure.

Let us deal with the facts. The only document that ever emerged purporting to be a CCC constitution was that comical document bearing your name. 
A serious political party constitution is not written around one individual by inserting that person’s name into it. If another legitimate CCC constitution existed, publish it in full and prove to Zimbabweans that I am an absolute liar.

I also said that CCC had no clearly defined leadership structure. You have now gone on Facebook and claimed that it did. So please publish the leadership organogram. Show Zimbabweans the national executive, the office bearers, their positions, their responsibilities, how they were appointed and to whom they were accountable.

More importantly, you yourself publicly stated on Twitter that CCC had no leadership positions. You specifically said that there was no secretary-general in CCC. Those were not my words. They were yours. At the time, you presented the absence of conventional leadership positions as an innovative feature of CCC. Today, you are claiming that CCC had leadership structures. Both statements cannot be true. Either you were lying then, or you are lying now. The contradiction is yours, not mine.

The only recognisable leadership positions were occupied by you as president, Fadzayi Mahere as spokesperson, whom you fired on the eve of the election on the advice of people in the army and CIO, and Ostallos as organising secretary and deputy spokesperson. Who were the other leaders, and where were they placed within the party’s organogram? Publish that organogram. You will not, because it did not exist.

This reinforces my earlier point; the job of journalists is not to cover up your political mess, Mr Chamisa. Our job is to seek and report the truth, ask difficult questions and hold every public figure accountable. Your job is to articulate your policies, organise your political movement and persuade Zimbabweans that you are capable of leading them.

When you make claims that are demonstrably untrue, journalists have a responsibility to challenge and expose them. So please shame me publicly by producing the CCC constitution that you say existed and the leadership organogram showing the structures you claim were in place. Publish both documents, and let Zimbabweans judge for themselves who is telling the truth.

And, by the way, my name is not Hopeful. My name is Hopewell.

#TruthIsInIt

text:
The Ministry of Road Transport and Highways has proposed making Vehicle-to-Vehicle (V2V) communication systems mandatory for specified vehicles. V2V can improve road safety by allowing vehicles to exchange information such as speed, position and direction to prevent collisions. But an always-on system can also create a new infrastructure for tracking and surveillance. (1/5)
Read More: https://t.co/YckNaxIuq6

We have also raised concerns about centralised authentication systems. If a central authority can link a pseudonymous vehicle identifier back to a real vehicle, it could potentially reconstruct who is travelling where and when. Privacy should therefore be built into the technical architecture through decentralised systems, including technologies such as zero-knowledge credentials and secure hardware. (4/5)

IFF has urged MoRTH to ensure that V2V data cannot be centrally logged, intercepted, retained or repurposed for tracking, surveillance or law enforcement without specific legal authorisation and judicial oversight. Independent security and privacy audits should happen before mandatory deployment, followed by periodic reviews of whether the mandate remains necessary and proportionate. Safer roads should not mean building a new surveillance infrastructure. (5/5)

NIXI has now given a third explanation for suspending https://t.co/6D4RZacQWP. First it was “Invalid WHOIS”. Then a “critical keyword”. Now, three weeks into the suspension, it says “Sansad” is a reserved term for Constitutional Authorities. But NIXI’s own reserved names list does not reserve “sansad” as a term, and https://t.co/6D4RZacQWP is not on it. (1/8)
Read More: https://t.co/BSrSHIC1hf

The purpose of reserved names is to prevent impersonation of public institutions. “Sansad” is also an ordinary Hindi word, and “Chalo Sansad” was the reported name of a public protest. The website expressly disclaimed any affiliation with Parliament or the Government. Reserving https://t.co/vWkHekQQYB for the official Digital Sansad website does not mean citizens cannot lawfully refer to Parliament in a domain name. (7/8)

Today, acting on the registrant’s instructions, IFF through Apar Gupta, Advocate sent a rejoinder to NIXI. We have placed the inconsistencies, the 2004 policy, NIXI’s own reserved-name lists, the RDAP comparison and the Aadhaar concerns on record. We have again demanded restoration, disclosure of the legal basis and any underlying orders, accountability for the Aadhaar collected, and functional grievance channels. As of 17 August, https://t.co/6D4RZacQWP remains suspended. We will publish any further response. (8/8)

IFF has written to the Union Home Secretary and the Census Commissioner over the household survey notified four days ago. Serial numbers 36 to 40 ask for mobile, Aadhaar, voter ID and passport numbers, not whether you have them, unlike serial number 40, which only asks about availability of a driving license.

IFF supports enumerating caste for substantive equality. But pairing Aadhaar numbers with religion and caste sits against the Aadhaar Act's bar on profiling, and the questionnaire itself remains unpublished.
We are not opposed to the census. We want it conducted in a way that earns public trust.
